“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Georgian PM: ‘Opposition’s current Russophobia is dictated by Global War Party’
World.content:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has published a lengthy social media statement linking Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine to Georgia‘s domestic politics and the country’s opposition.

According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Kobakhidze writes that after the war in Ukraine began in 2022, the “opposition’s pseudo-liberal minority” in Georgia adopted a radical stance towards Russia. He argues that such attitudes had not existed even after the August 2008 war, despite the fact that Russia continued to occupy 20% of Georgia’s territory.

In his statement, the prime minister recalls the consequences of the 2008 war. He says Russia’s military aggression killed 412 people, injured 2,232 others and displaced about 30,000 people. More than 120 Georgian settlements also remained beyond the occupation line.

Kobakhidze argues that the United National Movement, which was in power at the time, did not pursue a hard-line policy towards Russia. Instead, he says, it encouraged Russian tourists and investors to come to Georgia, promoted cultural and economic ties, facilitated Russian investment in various sectors and later unilaterally abolished visa requirements for Russian citizens.

According to the prime minister, neither government officials nor their supporters protested against that policy at the time. In this context, Kobakhidze names several current opposition politicians and public figures, including Elene Khoshtaria and Zurab Japaridze, and claims they supported closer relations with Russia during that period.

According to the prime minister, the opposition, along with affiliated NGOs and activists, turned into an “externally controlled network of agents” and adopted a sharply anti-Russian stance only after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Kobakhidze argues that the Georgian opposition’s current “Russophobia” is not genuine but stems from “directives issued by external forces”. He says that if anyone were to develop a truly radical attitude towards Russia, it should have happened after the August 2008 war, not after Russia’s second invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister concludes his statement by asking why this “network of agents” did not display the same attitude towards Russia after the 2008 war, but only after the war in Ukraine began. Kobakhidze says society “will easily find a logical explanation” for that question.

“I believe there is a question that must be asked and carefully considered by society. We all know that, both in the past and today, this network of agents in Georgia has acted on instructions from external forces, and that its homeland is not Georgia but the ‘deep state’.

Against that backdrop, it is worth asking why they were not instructed to promote Russophobia when there was the strongest possible reason to do so – after the August 2008 war – and why they have been instructed to do so now, when the victim of Russian aggression is not their formal homeland but another country, albeit a friendly one. I believe society will easily find a logical explanation for this contradiction,” Kobakhidze wrote.

Kobakhidze on Russophobia in Georgia

World.title: Diaspora youth: Patriots or ‘information soldiers’? The hidden mission of camp in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan. More than 120 young people from 64 countries gathered in Zangilan under the slogan “Reviving Cities”. Officials told participants they should defend Azerbaijan’s achievements and push back against what they described as “biased campaigns”.

Against the backdrop of protesters calling Ilham Aliyev a “dictator” in Berlin, that message raises another question: is the state seeking to foster independent thinkers or “information soldiers” who will promote its official narrative abroad?

What was discussed at the 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp?

The 7th Diaspora Youth Summer Camp, which opened in Zangilan on 2 August, is officially presented as a platform for “patriotic education”, learning about “the realities on the ground” and rejuvenating the Azerbaijani diaspora. More than 120 young people from 64 countries are spending a week visiting reconstruction projects in the territories retaken by Azerbaijan, meeting government officials and learning what organisers describe as “Azerbaijani realities”.

A closer look at the speeches by Fuad Muradov, chairman of the State Committee for Work with the Diaspora, and other officials, however, reveals a more pragmatic objective. The government appears to see young people living abroad not simply as members of the diaspora with ties to their homeland, but as active participants in the information battle.

Muradov said the participants should be able to “respond with well-founded arguments to biased campaigns”. He said they should “represent” Azerbaijan’s interests with dignity in their countries of residence, on international platforms and within their own communities.

Another message struck an even tougher tone. Officials said that although their number was small, some people living abroad who called themselves Azerbaijanis did not welcome Azerbaijan’s successes. They urged participants to know who these people were, be familiar with their statements and respond to them with well-reasoned arguments. Officials also said “black PR”, “distortion of facts” and “organised campaigns” were unacceptable. At the same time, they said they remained open to “well-founded criticism”.

Elvin Aslanov, a representative of the Heydar Aliyev Foundation, acknowledged that defending Azerbaijan abroad was “far from easy”, saying it required confronting double standards and disinformation. According to him, the young participants’ mission is to “convey the truth accurately and objectively”.

From the authorities’ perspective, such rhetoric may appear defensive and entirely legitimate. However, the broader context allows for another interpretation. Critics argue that the programme goes beyond patriotic education and instead systematically prepares “information soldiers” – young people expected to promote the official narrative on social media, in online discussions and in international debates. In other words, they see it as an attempt to build a state-directed “soft power” network.

What happened in Berlin, and why does it matter in this context?

The timing of these appeals is no coincidence. During Ilham Aliyev’s official visit to Germany on 21 July, Azerbaijani expatriates gathered on the streets of Berlin and chanted: “Dictator!”

Around the same time, Germany-based exiled blogger Alemdar Bunyatov approached Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev on a street in Berlin. He questioned them about political prisoners and allegations of torture.

Official media immediately described the incident as a “provocation” and portrayed Bunyatov as someone “known for his close ties to the Iranian intelligence services”. Responding to his questions, Bayramov dismissed the allegations of torture as “a personal opinion”.

Hajiyev, for his part, questioned Bunyatov about his sources of funding, his legal status in Germany and his reasons for leaving Azerbaijan. He stressed the importance of sovereignty and national security. The incident triggered a strong reaction in pro-government media, which portrayed the blogger’s questions as “provocative”.

The events in Berlin further illustrate the practical meaning of the messages delivered in Zangilan. In the official narrative, criticism is often framed as a “biased campaign”, “black PR” or the result of “external influence”.

As a result, the authorities themselves largely determine the line between “well-founded criticism” and a “biased campaign”. Young people, in turn, are expected to accept that distinction and challenge those whom the state places on the other side of it.

A method of training trolls?

Opposition figures and independent observers have long described such camps as a form of “troll factory”. Critics argue that their purpose is not to encourage independent thinking but to prepare young people to defend the official position on social media, in online discussions and before international audiences. They say that, under the banner of patriotism, organisers cultivate emotional attachment and ideological loyalty while encouraging participants to view critical voices as “hostile”.

Every country seeks to use its diaspora as a tool of soft power, and Azerbaijan is no exception. The problem, critics argue, is that the shrinking space for domestic criticism places a disproportionately heavy burden on young Azerbaijanis abroad to “defend” the official line. They must adapt to societies where freedom of expression is a fundamental principle while remaining loyal to Baku’s official narrative. For many young people, that contradiction can create genuine tension.

Muradov says, “We are open to dialogue”, while also insisting, “We will not tolerate black PR.” This raises an obvious question: what qualifies as “well-founded criticism”, and what counts as a “biased campaign”? If official media portray the questions and slogans heard on the streets of Berlin as a provocation, where is the line for young people who raise the same issues in international media or at academic forums?

Zangilan diaspora youth camp in Azerbaijan

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament holds first session as opposition, as expected, makes its presence felt
World.content:
First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

Armenia‘s newly elected parliament convened for the first time on 2 August. Three political forces won seats in the ninth National Assembly: the Civil Contract, Strong Armenia and Armenia factions. During the opening session, lawmakers managed only to appoint members of the Counting Commission. Heated exchanges between the ruling party and the opposition prevented them from addressing the rest of the agenda.

The opposition’s main grievance was the absence of the Catholicos from the opening session. The authorities did not invite him, and he did not bless the work of parliament. Opposition lawmakers described this as an unprecedented event in the history of independent Armenia.

Under the constitutional law governing the National Assembly’s rules of procedure, both the president and the Catholicos of All Armenians have the right to deliver opening remarks at parliament’s first session. This time, however, only President Vahagn Khachaturyan addressed lawmakers. Earlier, the Mother See of Holy Etchmiadzin said it had received no invitation for the Catholicos. When journalists asked Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan about Garegin II’s participation, he replied: “I do not know such a Catholicos.” The incident reflects the long-running dispute between the Armenian authorities and Catholicos of All Armenians Garegin II. More than two years ago, Prime Minister Pashinyan called for the Catholicos to step down. He initially argued that Garegin II could not lead the Armenian Apostolic Church because he had broken his vow of celibacy and fathered a daughter. Pashinyan later accused him of links with foreign intelligence services. The ruling Civil Contract party also included the removal of “the de facto head of the Church” in its election manifesto.

Lawmakers also fiercely debated the nomination of Ruben Rubinyan, the ruling party’s sole candidate for speaker of parliament.

Opposition MPs repeatedly referred to his research work at Istanbul Policy Center in Turkey in 2017–18. They asked whether he had interacted with local residents and even questioned what they looked like.

“Ask me directly whether I met representatives of the Turkish intelligence services in Turkey and whether they recruited me. Ask me: ‘Is that true?’ And I will answer: ‘No,'” Rubinyan said.

Parliament resumed its first session today. Lawmakers have already settled one of the main items on the agenda. In a secret ballot, they elected Ruben Rubinyan as speaker with 63 votes in favour and 28 against.

The opposition Armenia bloc boycotted the secret ballot. MPs from the second opposition force, the Strong Armenia faction, voted against Rubinyan’s nomination.

In the previous parliament, Rubinyan served as deputy speaker. Between 2022 and 2026, he also acted as Armenia’s special envoy for the normalisation of relations with Turkey. A few days ago, Rubinyan said he would be unable to continue in that role if parliament elected him speaker. The ruling party has not yet announced who will succeed him.

“Where is the Patriarch?” Opposition MPs visit him to receive his blessing

On the opening day of the session, opposition MPs began chanting, “Where is the Patriarch?” after the president’s address. During the oath-taking ceremony, they pointedly refused to stand or recite the oath. They said they were protesting the Catholicos’s absence. However, they signed the written text of the oath, allowing them to take office formally.

At the end of the first working day, MPs from both opposition factions visited the Catholicos’s residence.

The Mother See’s information service said Garegin II blessed the opposition lawmakers. He spoke of an “alarming situation and serious problems” facing the country. He also criticised what he described as the authorities’ “illegal and unconstitutional actions” against the Church.

Catholicos receives opposition MPs at the Mother See

The Catholicos praised what he described as the opposition MPs’ “devotion and filial love for the Church”. He said their stance was especially important at a time when “the authorities continue their campaign of repression, while national benefactor Samvel Karapetyan remains under arrest for speaking out in defence of Holy Etchmiadzin”.

In June last year, Armenian authorities opened a criminal case against Russian businessman and billionaire Samvel Karapetyan. Prosecutors accused him of publicly calling for the seizure and usurpation of power. In an interview with local media, Karapetyan discussed the escalating conflict between the government and the Church. He said he supported the Church and added: “If Armenia’s political forces fail to resolve this situation, we will have to intervene in the campaign against the Church in our own way.” His supporters founded the Strong Armenia party after his arrest, and he has remained under house arrest since December last year.

105 MPs in the new parliament

The three political forces that entered the National Assembly secured the following number of seats:

The ruling Civil Contract party – 64 seats

The Strong Armenia faction – 29 seats

The Armenia bloc – 12 seats

Strong Armenia leader and businessman Samvel Karapetyan did not enter parliament. During the election campaign, his allies confidently predicted victory and even said Karapetyan would become prime minister. However, he is ineligible to serve either as an MP or as prime minister. Under Armenia’s constitution, anyone holding citizenship of another country cannot hold either office. Karapetyan holds Armenian, Russian and Cypriot citizenship.

Former President Robert Kocharyan headed the electoral list of the Armenia bloc, making him its candidate for prime minister. However, Kocharyan declined to take up his parliamentary seat. His son, Levon Kocharyan, who also ran on the bloc’s list, accepted a mandate and has already joined parliament. He also served as an MP for the Armenia bloc in the previous legislature.

“I will do everything to ensure our children never experience war”

Rubinyan thanked the more than 700,000 voters who backed Civil Contract. He said they had given the ruling party “a mandate to continue Armenia’s democratic reforms and peace agenda”. According to Rubinyan, those voters had defended the country’s sovereignty and independence.

He said the time had come for Armenians to enjoy peaceful lives, have children and raise them without fear.

“My son, who is almost two years old, and children of his age have never experienced war. I will do everything to ensure that my children, your children and all our children never have to learn what war is,” he said.

Rubinyan also thanked those who voted for opposition parties out of conviction rather than in exchange for election bribes.

“It is time to change the political discourse,” Rubinyan says

Addressing opposition MPs, Rubinyan raised the issue of the tone of parliamentary debate. He said society, political circles and journalists had formed a common view of parliament in recent months. According to him, many now see the National Assembly as a place for pointless arguments, slander and insults.

“They say this parliament will be even worse than the previous one in that respect. It seems everyone expects exactly that from us. I want to propose that we break this curse together,” the speaker said.

He argued that the opposition factions had largely stayed away from the work of the previous, eighth convocation of parliament.

“All we saw here was political confrontation, shouting and radical speeches. It is time to change the narratives that have dominated Armenian politics over the past six years. I propose that we make this parliament a place for vigorous but respectful debate that never crosses the boundaries of decency.”

At the same time, he warned that if the opposition rejected his proposal and continued “down the well-trodden path”, the ruling party was ready to respond “in the toughest possible way”.

“Why did we take our seats?” Opposition MPs explain

Ishkhan Saghatelyan, an MP from the Armenia faction, argued that neither the opposition nor the ruling party had truly won the election.

He again claimed that the authorities had used administrative resources during the campaign and imprisoned opposition figures.

“This parliament has a serious legitimacy problem. We are here to organise political struggle and advance national goals. We are here to raise the concerns of Armenia’s citizens, speak about the prisoners held in Baku and Armenia’s occupied territories, and, yes, defend the people of Artsakh’s right to a collective return.”

Hayk Farmanyan, an MP from the Strong Armenia faction, echoed that message.

“We accepted our mandates to remain true to our Armenian identity, to fight for our national values, and to defend our dignity, our identity and our Church.”

Comment

Political analyst Lilit Dallakyan shared her impressions of the new parliament’s opening session on social media:

“Well, I ‘congratulate’ the Armenian people on the start of work by a new, high-quality, substantive parliament that is supposedly ready to tackle Armenia’s complex challenges.

The daily exchange of ‘Your father is a murderer’ [directed at MP Levon Kocharyan, son of former President Robert Kocharyan] will now gain a new, equally substantive argument: ‘Your uncle is a Russian oligarch’ [directed at MP Narek Karapetyan, nephew of Strong Armenia leader Samvel Karapetyan]. That will, in turn, prompt the reply: ‘You are Turkish dictators’ [directed at the authorities].

The only positive aspect is that this season of the series is unlikely to interest anyone or distract people from the real problems that are rapidly emerging.

At a time of profound change across the world, Armenian society and every individual will have to look for solutions to their own problems. Ultimately, that will bring about the changes the country needs.”

First session of Armenia’s ninth parliament

World.title: Opinion: ‘Abkhaz diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive’
World.content:
Against the backdrop of the Pacific island nation of Nauru withdrawing its recognition of Abkhazia’s independence, prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania reflects on what Abkhazia’s foreign policy doctrine should look like.

Nauru, a small island nation in the Pacific region of Micronesia, recognised Abkhazia’s independence in 2009 but withdrew that recognition in late July 2026. The move reduced the number of countries recognising Abkhazia’s independence to four. Abkhazia’s foreign ministry said Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure”.

Akhra Bzhania said: “Around 230,000 irregular migrants crossed the EU’s borders in 2025–26 alone. All of them fled countries that enjoy broad international recognition.

Why didn’t they stay in Morocco, Mali or Afghanistan? Presumably because having a flag outside the UN headquarters does not automatically mean you live in a genuine state – one where you can influence public life, where your voice matters and where your dignity will never be trampled.

Being a recognised country and being a country where people want to live and are willing to die for it are two different things.

You may achieve the first and never attain the second. But if you have the second, then you have accomplished the most important task: building a country that belongs to its citizens. That is what defines a modern state. And that is precisely what should become the main instrument for Abkhazia’s integration into the international community.

Bzhania continued: “We must send a clear message to the international community that, despite sanctions, isolation and the threat of war, the people of Abkhazia have built a society based on the rule of law and freedom. Without being members of international institutions, we have incorporated the core principles of international conventions on civil and political rights into our system of governance.

We see ourselves as part of the international community and believe we deserve our rightful place within it. To achieve that, our diplomacy must become more flexible – and more assertive. It should focus not on waiting for or preserving acts of recognition, but on consistently demonstrating our statehood and expanding our international contacts.

No one else is obliged to do this for us. By recognising our sovereignty, Russia effectively made Abkhazia a subject of international law. But it cannot solve our problems on our behalf.”

Bzhania continued: “We must use every tool at our disposal to achieve our goals: the resources of the diaspora, cultural, trade and sporting ties, personal connections, migration policy and regional logistics. In this game, we need to keep raising the stakes.

Today, there is a window of opportunity for such an active policy. It is no secret that relations between Georgia and the West are at their lowest point since the 1990s. Those on whom Tbilisi relied to promote its anti-Abkhaz agenda have become disillusioned with Georgia, and we should take advantage of that. That includes reviving the active dialogue with European countries that existed in the late 1990s. After all, the hopes the West once placed in Georgia as a bastion of the free world in the Caucasus have, to a greater extent, been realised in Abkhazia.

Another key asset, which has remained almost entirely outside our foreign policy efforts, is the Circassian diaspora. Four million people spread across 50 countries represent a powerful resource we can genuinely rely on. More importantly, we should offer them the prospect of political cooperation.

Abkhazia can and should become the centre of the Circassian world as the only independent state of this sub-ethnic group. Our country can become the same kind of homeland for Circassians worldwide that Israel has become for Jews. If every Circassian, wherever they live, knows they will find protection and support for their interests in Abkhazia, it will create a strong foundation for advancing our shared interests.”

Bzhania concluded: “It will probably not happen tomorrow, no matter how much effort we put in. But it can happen within a foreseeable future if those efforts remain consistent and systematic.

In 2017, I had the honour of welcoming a delegation from Nauru’s parliament to Abkhazia on behalf of the Abkhaz parliament. They were wonderful, warm people. Unfortunately, ships at sea do not only meet – they also part ways. Today, Nauru has set a course away from Abkhazia, apparently believing it to be the safer option. I wish them well. As for us, we will continue on our own course.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Nauru’s withdrawal of recognition of Abkhazia

World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: Stokes claims cricket has drinking culture, not just England
World.content:
Former England captain Ben Stokes has hit back at claims his side had a drinking problem, instead claiming cricket as a sport has a drinking culture.

Stokes, who abruptly retired in June, appeared on a podcast with former England teammate Stuart Broad where he addressed a range of different topics.

Among those was a suggestion that England's team has a drinking problem after a number of off-field incidents during last summer's ill-fated Ashes tour to Australia.

"God, that's such an extreme thing to put on a team," Stokes told Broad on the For Love Of Cricket podcast when asked whether England had a drinking problem.

Ben Stokes's retirement a perfect example of his main character energy Ben Stokes has been the centre of England's cricketing universe for 15 years. In announcing his retirement mid-match, he highlighted how damaging that main character energy can be.

"I think cricket has just a drinking culture and it hasn't changed. We're in 2026 where the game has gone more professional over the years, and one thing that I think has just stayed within cricket is its relationship with alcohol, from club cricket and then works its way up. It's just stayed there and it's been embedded within the sport.

"The relationship with alcohol and cricket is just something that hasn't moved on as the game of cricket has become more professional.

"There's been more science and medicine, there's more nutritional information, there's more this, there's more that, but the one thing that has been a constant and stayed around and has been for a very long time is its relationship with alcohol.

"So for people who think that the English cricket team has a drinking culture, I'd say no.

" I would just say cricket has culture that is associated with alcohol. "

England's team under Stokes faced heavy criticism during its mid-Ashes break in Noosa last year, which came with the team already in an 0-2 hole.

Opener Ben Duckett was filmed by fans while heavily intoxicated and struggling to find his way back to England's hotel, while during the final Test in Sydney, it emerged that vice-captain Harry Brook had gotten into an altercation with a bouncer on the team's New Zealand tour.

"I think it can be a problem," Stokes said of cricket's drinking culture.

"If you look at everything over the years, you look at a lot of people that have been involved within cricket and have had bad relationships with alcohol. It's just, I don't know what you do to change it."

Ben Stokes's Ashes understudy Harry Brook (right) was involved in an altercation with a nightclub bouncer in New Zealand prior to the Ashes. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley/ECB)

Stokes also referenced his own personal experience with alcohol throughout his career.

He was arrested in 2017 after his involvement in a street brawl near a nightclub with then-teammate Alex Hales and served an eight-match suspension for the incident.

"I've had … I don't want to say problems, but I've had relationships with alcohol at times over my career that have been potentially dangerous, if that makes sense, but it's completely different to me now," he said.

"I just think that there's this relationship with alcohol within cricket that has been the same from the 80s.

Former Australian Test batter David Boon (centre) has become well known for his love of beer, namely the 52 he consumed on a flight to the UK. (Getty Images: PA Images)

"As the game has got better and better and better, that thing has just stayed around. That's my opinion on cricket and alcohol."

Stokes's theory regarding cricket and its athletes' relationship to alcohol is not without credence.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

In Australian cricket, the story of David Boon drinking 52 beers on a flight to the UK ahead of the 1989 Ashes series is spoken about as the stuff of legend.

Boon appeared on a podcast in 2023 saying he regretted the whole episode.

"I've got to be brutally honest here, I won't deny it happened. We all do stupid things in our lives and I'll finish by just being serious," he said on the BackChat Sports Show.

"You have fun, you do something and then you think: 'Shit, what about the ramifications to everything else', to your family, to your children.

""It caused some crap over the years, and it's something that I regret a lot. Can't deny it but I do regret it. And I was stupid to be able to do that when you're in the public eye."

World.title: Gas giant prosecuted after under-reporting toxic emissions
World.content:
The Northern Territory's environmental regulator has charged Japanese gas giant Inpex for under-reporting the amount of toxic emissions it released from the Ichthys facility near Darwin.

The NT Environment Protection Authority (EPA) said it decided to prosecute after Inpex told the regulator it had significantly under-reported the level of benzene and toluene emissions between 2019 and 2024.

In a statement, the NT EPA said the under-reporting allegedly represented a breach of Inpex's environmental licence to operate.

"The NT EPA licences Ichthys LNG through an environment protection licence, originally granted on 13 December 2017," the statement said.

"Under the licence, Ichthys LNG is required to annually report total emissions to air in tonnes to the NT EPA.

"In October 2025, Ichthys LNG informed the NT EPA of significant under-reporting of emissions from the Ichthys LNG facility. The NT EPA has now commenced prosecution in relation to this matter."

The NT EPA recently recommended changes to the licences of Darwin's two major gas processing companies, Santos and Inpex, after Inpex's under-reporting triggered a review.

The NT EPA said it would not provide further comment while the matter is before the courts.

It is understood the matter will appear in Darwin Local Court, but a date is yet to be finalised.

Inpex was contacted for comment.

More to come.

World.title: Woman charged with murder after death of 'malnourished' non-verbal man
World.content:
A south Brisbane woman has been charged over the death of a non-verbal man who police said was "malnourished".

Isaac Oar, also known as 'Ike', was found unresponsive at an address in Ayr in North Queensland on August 10, 2023, in what first responders described as a "confronting" situation.

The 56-year-old was pronounced dead at the scene.

Mr Oar had Down Syndrome and was a recipient of the National Insurance Disability Scheme (NDIS).

Police said they conducted a "complex" investigation into Mr Oar's death, finding he was experiencing serious malnourishment and weighed just 29kg at the time of his death.

At the time, Detective Inspector Jason Shepherd said Mr Oar hadn't received any professional medical treatment in well over a decade.

"He was only 29 kilos — that doesn't happen overnight," he said.

"There has obviously been years of neglect in some format."

Police said they had investigated his health, care and treatment throughout his life.

On Tuesday, detectives from the Crime Command Homicide Investigation Unit and Ayr Criminal Investigation Branch arrested a 70-year-old woman from Forest Lake and charged her with one count of murder (domestic violence).

She is expected to appear in Brisbane Magistrates Court today.

World.title: Man arrested at Trump golf course carrying ammunition, authorities say
World.content:
An armed man was arrested at US President Donald Trump's Los Angeles golf course on Sunday, local time, after appearing to monitor security preparations two days ahead of a fundraiser, authorities say.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department said Jeanine John Taele, 38, was taking photos and video and had a 16-round magazine with ammunition in his pocket. Authorities recovered a loaded pistol in his car.

Law enforcement searched his home in the nearby city of Downey on Monday and found a plethora of firearms, magazines and ammunition, body armour and notebooks with "concerning statements".

A jury in 2025 found a man guilty of trying to assassinate Donald Trump at the president’s Florida country club. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

The sheriff's department announced the arrest as Mr Trump was preparing to arrive for a Republican National Committee fundraising dinner at the Trump National Golf Course in the suburb of Rancho Palos Verdes just south of Los Angeles.

The department did not elaborate on what the notebooks' "concerning statements" were or whether the man was planning an attack on the president or event.

Political violence continues to ring through American history The third assassination attempt on US President Donald Trump thrust the country's long history of political violence into the spotlight.

Mr Taele was charged with several felonies, including second-degree robbery, receiving a large-capacity magazine and possession of a short-barrelled rifle or shotgun. He was also charged with carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle, a misdemeanour.

He pleaded not guilty to all the charges and was ordered to stay away from the golf course and not possess weapons. His bail was set at $US250,000 ($354,600).

It was unclear whether he had a lawyer, and family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

The sheriff's department said when they made contact with Mr Taele on Sunday, they had determined he was being investigated by the El Segundo Police Department for robbery.

The sheriff's department said there is "no credible threat to our communities".

A jury in 2025 found a man guilty of trying to assassinate Mr Trump at the president's Florida country club.

AP

World.title: High Court throws out reduced sentence for teen who killed Emma Lovell
World.content:
A reduced jail sentence handed to a 17-year-old over the murder of Brisbane woman Emma Lovell has been thrown out by the High Court.

The mother of two died after she and her husband Lee were stabbed in a burglary at their home on Boxing Day in 2022.

Her killer, now in his 20s, pleaded guilty to four charges, including murder, and was originally sentenced to 14 years in prison.

That was reduced by 60 per cent by the Queensland Court of Appeal, because of special circumstances, including his age and guilty plea.

But today, the High Court unanimously allowed the appeal, finding it was not open for the Court of Appeal to interfere with the original sentencing judge based on the principle of judicial restraint.

Appeal court 'undermined' statutory scheme: solicitor-general

The original judge imposed a sentence of 14 years in March 2024.

Under the law at the time, children could only be held for 70 per cent of their sentence, although that could be reduced in special circumstances.

The sentencing judge, Justice Tom Sullivan, described the murder as "particularly heinous" and determined special circumstances did not apply.

But the Queensland Court of Appeal disagreed, and reduced the time the teen would spend in custody to 60 per cent on the basis the sentence was excessive.

Lee and Emma Lovell had been married for two decades when she was killed. (Facebook: Lee Lovell)

The Queensland Attorney-General brought the case to the High Court in April, where the state's Solicitor-General, Gim Del Villar, argued the Court of Appeal applied the wrong standard to its revision.

"The appeal court undermined the statutory scheme," Mr Del Villar said.

Lawyers for the killer rejected that, claiming the sentencing judge had faulted by letting the seriousness of the offending overwhelm the mitigating factors that should have discounted the sentence, including his disadvantaged upbringing, age, and guilty plea.

Ms Lovell's husband, Lee, who was injured in the attack, travelled to Canberra for the High Court hearing in April this year.

"I just think I owe it to Emma, really, to see this through," he said at the time.

"I've been there from the start, and I'll continue on as long as it takes really to get justice for her and maybe for the girls and I, too."

World.title: High Court rules in favour of native title holders fighting NT water licence
World.content:
Native title holders from Central Australia have won their fight to assert cultural rights over an aquifer located on their lands.

The High Court of Australia today decided in favour of the Mpwerempwer Aboriginal Corporation (MAC), which had challenged a plan to turn thousands of hectares on Singleton Station, south of Tennant Creek, into an irrigated horticulture business.

The station's lessees, Fortune Agribusiness, plan to grow mandarins, table grapes, avocados, muskmelons, and other fruits.

The endeavour would transform the cattle property into one of the nation's biggest fruit farms, requiring 40,000 megalitres (40 billion litres) of water every year once fully developed.

That demand was at the heart of the appeal brought by MAC, which submitted that water was only available from an underground aquifer accessed by bores on the property.

It claimed water, and sites traditionally associated with access to or use of water, have significance for traditional occupants of arid lands.

The traditional owners say they are concerned the licence will lead to the destruction of too many sacred water sites. (Supplied: Anna Miers, Central Land Council)

Claim water licence had not been lawfully granted

The 2020 application by Fortune for the 30-year water licence was described by the Department of Environment at the time as being "possibly the largest volume application in a single water resource by a single entity in Australia".

Lawyers for MAC claimed the water licence had not been lawfully granted because the minister in charge did not properly justify granting the water licence for 30 years rather than the standard 10-year period.

They also argued Aboriginal cultural values had not been considered in the making of that decision, and that native title holders had been denied procedural fairness by decision makers.

MAC, which is made up of traditional owners and native title holders from four Aboriginal landholding groups, had failed in their bid to overturn the licence in challenges heard by the Northern Territory Supreme Court and Court of Appeal over the last four years.

The native title and traditional owners said they were concerned the licence would lead to the destruction of too many sacred water sites and affect native plants and animals that depend on the water.

In February, traditional owner Valerie Ngapangardi Curtis said the licence would be damaging in multiple ways.

"If they take too much water, it's going to damage our country, it's going to damage all our plants and animals, and it's going to damage our culture as well and dreaming and storyline," she said.

The NT government said in its submissions the law does not require the decision-maker to consider the impact on Aboriginal cultural values. (ABC Alice Springs: Samantha Jonscher)

Minister denied MAC procedural fairness, court finds

For its part, the Northern Territory government and Fortune had argued the minister responsible was not legally obliged to consider special circumstances, including any cultural values impact assessment.

But today, the High Court unanimously agreed the water licence had not been lawfully granted by the Northern Territory government.

It found the minister had not properly satisfied circumstances that justified the extended 30-year licence, and that the minister had denied MAC procedural fairness in not providing a reasonable opportunity to make its case about conditions imposed on the licence.

The decision means the water licence will be quashed and the process referred back to the minister responsible, who will also have to consider the territory's environmental approvals processes associated with the site.

The NT government must also pay the costs of MAC's appeal, but limited only to those that went towards its arguments about procedural fairness, with the Supreme Court to determine other costs.

World.title: Hobart wharf demolition paving way for new icebreaker berth
World.content:
A "complex" operation to deconstruct an aging wharf in Hobart has begun, paving the way for a new home berth for Australia's Antarctic icebreaker, RSV Nuyina.

The Macquarie Wharf 6 demolition is part of a broader wharf redevelopment project aimed at modernising Tasmania's port network and providing a marine base for Australia's Antarctic program.

TasPorts CEO Allan Gray said more than 12,900 tonnes of concrete, steel and timber would be "carefully separated, broken down and removed".

"Deconstructing a structure of this size over water is a genuinely complex undertaking," Captain Gray said.

The demolition works are expected to take five months. (Supplied: www.robburnettimages.com)

Specialised marine equipment will be used, from a 280-tonne crawler crane to excavators fitted with rock breakers, shears and pulverisers.

"With works taking place on the River Derwent, environmental controls, including protective silt curtains and marine-life monitoring, are in place to protect the local environment throughout the works," Captain Gray said.

The wharf, which was riddled with concrete cancer, will be demolished in sections, followed by construction and piling for the new wharf.

The project received $188 million from the federal government.

Surrounding wharves will also be upgraded. (Supplied: www.robburnettimages.com)

Federal Member for Franklin Julie Collins said it was "terrific" to see the project underway.

" Hobart is a crucial hub for Antarctic and Southern Ocean science in Australia. We're proud to be investing in Tasmania to ensure it remains our gateway to Antarctica for years to come. "

Wharves 4 and 5 will also be upgraded as part of the wider works.

Nuyina's refuelling saga ongoing

The redevelopment of the wharf into the new home berth for RSV Nuyina is due for completion in 2028.

But the state and federal governments are yet to agree on a solution for Nuyina's expensive and lengthy refuelling journey to Burnie in the state's north-west.

The icebreaker must travel 674 kilometres, costing almost $900,000 extra each year, because it is unable to refuel at Selfs Point, a few kilometres from its Macquarie Wharf home port.

This is due to a ban on the ship travelling under the Tasman Bridge, after TasPorts' harbourmaster determined Nuyina lacked the "directional stability" required for a safe transit under the bridge.

In 1975, the Tasman Bridge partially collapsed after an ore carrier struck the pylons, causing the deaths of 12 people.

The state government promised in 2024 to find a refuelling solution as part of the Macquarie Wharf upgrade deal with the Commonwealth.

Speaking today, Tasmania's Infrastructure and Transport Minister Kerry Vincent said discussions were in the final stages.

World.title: Growers find expanding markets to save bumper avocado crop from oversupply
World.content:
The avocado industry is experiencing another high-volume crop year, but unlike previous years with oversupply, the fruit is finding a market.

Increasing domestic consumption and record export volumes have helped absorb the bumper harvest, a stark turnaround from just a few seasons ago when the market struggled to cope with high production.

The Avocado Collective, which markets and supports avocado growers across Australia, said the industry was strategic in selling this year's crop.

The group's Brent Chambers said during the opening weeks of Queensland's Shepard avocado season, which typically ran from February to April, almost the entire crop was exported.

"We see there's great value in exporting Shepards early, removing them from the domestic market to ensure that growers get the best economic return," he said.

Brent Chambers says the industry is sending more early fruit out for export. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Far North Queensland grower and Avocados Australia director Lawrence Massasso said rising domestic consumption had improved the industry's ability to handle large crops.

"During the Shepard season we had supply up around 600 to 650,000 trays a week, which two or three seasons ago we would have said that was impossible to clear [but] that fruit cleared every week," he said.

"We have more and more really committed [Australian] customers who will continue to support us come hell or high water."

The volume of fruit coming to market has resulted in lower prices, with Shepard avocados retailing for as low as 90 cents per piece.

"We weren't [making good money]. But the fruit was clearing and growers were getting a return on that crop," Mr Massasso said.

Lawrence Massasso says domestic consumption has increased significantly in the past few years. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Export numbers

Rabobank senior analyst Michael Harvey said national production could reach about 170,000 metric tonnes in coming seasons, with Queensland continuing to produce about half of Australia's crop.

"Queensland's still the largest producing state … we're still heading towards a record production in the coming years and that will mean greater exports as well," he said.

Up to 30 per cent of the national crop was exported this season, with record numbers sent overseas.

Hong Kong, Singapore and Malaysia remain key markets, while Japan and Thailand continue to emerge.

By the end of June, Australian avocado exports were more than 50 per cent higher than the same time last year.

Mr Harvey said global demand was keeping pace with rising production.

"Global avocado exports are continuing to grow at a rapid rate. In fact, in the last 15 years, you've seen a fourfold expansion in global exports of avocado," Mr Harvey said.

"Global avocado consumption is growing, there is obviously increasing production to meet that growing demand."

Rabobank says national production of avocados could reach about 170,000 metric tonnes. (ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson)

Smaller crop in 2027

Western Australia is the country's second largest producing state.

Mr Chambers said this year it produced about 13.5 million trays of avocados, but next year, that number was expected to drop significantly to 5 million trays.

It was due to behaviour cycles in the crop, where after a strong yielding year, the trees typically produced less fruit.

Mr Chambers said the smaller crop was likely to lift supermarket prices nationally, particularly during summer.

"[Prices] are going to be pretty buoyant during that January, February period," he said.

However, he expected production to rebound in 2028 as Western Australia and north Queensland returned with strong crops.

"Again, the strategy will be how much can we move offshore," he said.

"If we start developing those relationships now, hopefully we can keep that price relatively high."

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination continues of complainant on third day of alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: What HSC economics students ask Ross Gittins the most
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC What HSC economics students ask Ross Gittins the most Emily Kowal August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At the end of every year, like clockwork, Ross Gittins’ inbox fills with the same request, sent by a year 12 economics student: Could he please post them a signed photo of himself? Their teacher is a big fan. “I am the rock star of high school economics. It is absurd,” Gittins laughs. For five decades, economics students have turned to The Sydney Morning Herald economics editor’s columns to prepare for their exams and assignments. Now, they have had the chance to ask Gittins, and his protégée, economics writer Millie Muroi, their economics questions as they prepare for their trials and final exams. The questions were varied and broad. Riley Hughes from Cranbrook School asked how the government should balance taxes on cigarettes given the illicit tobacco black market, while Layne Phillips from Pymble Ladies’ College asked Gittins and Muroi how young people should deal with exorbitant house prices.



“Is it important that we stay optimistic and continue working within the system, or is the level of housing affordability and inaccessibility a reason for us to be more critical and push for change?” Layne asked. In response, Gittins said young people should “stay within the system” but fight for change. “The system has been allowed to run in a way that gives a lot of benefit to people who already own a home. It’s wonderful for me, but it’s not wonderful for some young person who might want to buy my house,” said Gittins. “The risk we have with this is we have a generation of young people who say the system is biased against us, we are going to put up a fight against the system. It’s your system as much as it is all the oldies’. What we need to do is change that system so that it gives everybody, particularly young people, a better deal.”



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy Your boss will hate this economic fix … but you’ll love it Ross Gittins Economics Editor Emily Wu from Hornsby Girls High asked whether we should change the way we measure the health of Australia’s labour market. “As AI and automation begin to replace labour, do you believe we should put more emphasis on labour under-utilisation data to better understand the true capacity of the Australian workforce?” Wu asked. Amid declining enrolments in HSC economics, Gittins praised the subject. “The great strength of high school economics is that it’s so closely based on current events,” he said.



“When you actually study it, rather than think about studying it, you find out it’s quite interesting, and it gets you engaged in the political process in a way that most HSC subjects don’t.” Check out everything students asked Gittins and Muroi here. World.title: Jenolan Caves is set to reopen. But getting there is going to be tricky
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Jenolan Caves is set to reopen. But getting there is going to be tricky Julie Power August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW’s Jenolan Caves is scheduled to reopen early next year, after six years of natural disasters that caused catastrophic damage to access roads, the precinct and the historic mountain retreat Caves House. But long-term access to the site has yet to be finalised, and it is unlikely that vehicles will be allowed into the precinct again, or to enter via the Grand Arch, as they did for decades. Jenolan Caves Reserve Trust director Andrew Le Lievre hopes the public can return, even though the roads may never reopen. Wolter Peeters Before Jenolan reopens, the state government is expected to consider a range of alternate transport options including a $44 million detachable gondola, a cable car similar to the one used at Taronga Zoo in Sydney. It would transport visitors from the escarpment to the valley through 1154 metres. Jenolan Caves Reserve Trust director Andrew Le Lievre said he was working with Transport for NSW on providing a fleet of shuttle buses that could carry hundreds of visitors from a parking lot at the top of the hill.



“Our preferred option is not to have the public driving on that road. It is very steep, it is very narrow and it’s very windy,” he said. The member for Bathurst Paul Toole said a gondola from the Two Mile Road section of Jenolan Caves Road to Caves House was a “no-brainer solution” that would resolve financial and geographical issues. “A gondola will add to the magical experience of Jenolan Caves and offer a new perspective as visitors glide down the valley,” Toole said. The cost and reliability of the gondola was the preferred option in a report by consultants Riser + Gain. It was the most cost-effective and the least damaging for biodiversity and the limestone. The report estimated that it would cost at least $150 million to fix the Five Mile section of Jenolan Caves Road. Even then it would still be vulnerable to land slips. It is still closed and Transport for NSW is expected to make a final decision on the viability of future repairs in the next few months.



Repairs to the Two Mile section of Jenolan Caves Road were estimated at more than $57 million and are expected to be completed this year, depending on weather. In future it will serve as an access road. Related Article Roads ‘Mind-blowing’: How a convict-built crossing closed a Blue Mountains highway Victoria Pass is also currently closed on the Great Western Highway between Mount Victoria and Little Hartley, causing further delays for visitors from Sydney and the Blue Mountains. Following upgrades and restoration works across the site, Le Lievre said visitors would be able to visit caves that hadn’t been open to the public for years. These include: the Ribbon, famous for its gravity-defying helictites; the Jubilee, with its rich crystal displays; and the River Cave, described as a “mind-bending labyrinth”. Guides would escort visitors to give them a sense of wonder and awe that came with discovering something new to them yet older than 340 million years.



Le Lievre said: “One of our major challenges has been that people have been to the caves usually as schoolchildren and they feel that that’s the experience, only to come back with potentially children or grandchildren.” Paul Toole, member for Bathurst, visting Jenolan Caves. Paul Toole MP Toole said the reopening of Jenolan Caves would provide a significant boost to local businesses, jobs and the wider regional economy. It was one of the region’s “greatest natural treasures for generations, drawing visitors from across Australia and around the world”. The oldest open cave system in the world also has a new attraction: a chance for the public to spot one of the world’s latest discoveries, a cave cricket about the size of a coffee bean. Known as the Jenolan Cave Cricket, it is called the Speleotettix binoomea, a reference to the traditional Indigenous name for Jenolan that means dark spaces. It is the first time a word used by the traditional Gundungurra people has been used to describe a species.



Researchers have recently described a new species of cave cricket, found within the cave systems of Jenolan, Wombeyan and Abercrombie. Dr Anne Musser Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the cricket’s discovery was “a powerful reminder of the area’s unique natural and cultural significance”. After the pandemic the caves attracted fewer than 50,000 visitors a year, compared with 240,000 a year, on average, before then. After assessing other options, including a funicular, the report recommended a mono-detachable gondola that could transport about 900 visitors per hour per direction (1800 in total), or about 500,000 a year in the short term and more if needed later. The absence of vehicles for six years from the site, combined with National Parks’ work to remove feral animals, had helped re-establish brushed tail possums, which were on the brink of extinction in 1988. Other native animals had flourished, including the spotted-tailed quoll and a family of three platypus in the Blue Lake.

World.title: Cyclists accused of ‘faking larger bra size’ at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
SportTour de France Cyclists accused of ‘faking larger bra size’ at Tour de France Femmes Tom Cary and Jeremy Wilson August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A row has broken out at the Tour de France Femmes following allegations some riders are artificially exaggerating their bust size to gain a “bra booster” aerodynamic advantage for the time trial. Riders were checked before the fourth stage of the Tour on Tuesday by officials to ensure they were not wearing padded bras or hiding other objects between their chest and clothing. At least one rider was seen being checked pre-stage by a male official, accompanied by a female witness. The peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the women’s Tour de France. AP According to WielerFlits, a leading cycling news platform in the Netherlands and Belgium, “several” women’s WorldTour teams have raised concerns riders are padding their bras to “fake” a larger cup size. How does ‘bra boosting’ work?



Referred to as “chest fairing”, increasing the surface area of the chest can change the airflow around the cyclist during the time trial and create a measurable benefit over multiple kilometres. Bert Blocken, professor of aerodynamics at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland and LUT in Finland, who has produced studies on the subject, said he had been sent photographs that “seemed to suggest that there are indeed some objects that some female riders stick behind their shirt”. Blocken added that “it was definitely a concern with the men’s races in 2023 and 2024”, which was then addressed in a scientific article he had published. Blocken said he had also talked to the International Cycling Union (UCI), the world governing body for the sport, about the issues. Titled “Analysis of chest fairings in time trial cycling” the scientific review found chest fairing can give a 3.6 per cent drag reduction and concluded that “time gains by chest fairing can decide who wins or loses a time trial”.



Blocken’s article defines chest-fairing as when “some cyclists in triathlon and road cycling competitions have been riding with an object stuck between their chest and their shirt, attempting to reduce aerodynamic drag”. The most excessive examples had previously occurred in triathlon, with the use of water bottles. Blocken wrote that “cyclists, cycling teams and cycling product manufacturers are constantly looking for aerodynamic improvements that can withstand the scrutiny of the UCI”. Blocken stressed that he does not follow women’s cycling closely but said he had been shown the photographs by a journalist from WielerFlits. Both the UCI and the Tour de France Femmes were approached for comment before Tuesday’s time trial. The teams WielerFlits spoke to anonymously believe the UCI should have a female official check the riders immediately after the time trial in a closed tent to ensure they are not concealing anything in their bra or under their aero clothing.



Why would a larger bust help in time trialling? It might sound counterintuitive that a “larger” skinsuit would help to produce an aerodynamic advantage. Would not wrinkles or loose, baggy fabric slow a rider down? Well, yes they would. But the theory behind artificially inflating your bust is that by altering the shape of the chest, a rider can create a better airflow underneath a perfectly tight skinsuit. In time trials, riders adopt a tucked position with their forearms close together over their bars. This creates a pocket or “valley” between the helmet, shoulders and chest. Air flowing into that depression can separate and become turbulent, increasing drag. Netherlands’ Lorena Wiebes of team SD Worx Protime, centre, crosses the finish line to win the second stage of the women’s tour from Aigle to Geneva. AP By adding carefully shaped padding to the chest, the front of the rider becomes rounder and smoother, guiding the airflow cleanly around the body.



Blocken’s thesis, published on ScienceDirect two years ago, concluded that riders could achieve a reduction in air resistance of up to 3.6 per cent when using an object in the optimal shape that covers the chest. This translates into a time saving of at least 0.78 seconds per kilometre. Why is “chest fairing” controversial? Artificially altering clothing is prohibited by the (UCI). If a rider is caught during or after a race and in violation of UCI’s regulations, they could face immediate disqualification and fined. Before Tuesday’s time trial, race organisers announced they would attempt to prevent any scandal from arising by requiring riders to report for bike and outfit checks at least 10 minutes before the start of the fourth stage. In their stage three jury report, organisers added: “Pre-checks on riders’ equipment (race and spare bikes, their respective accessories and devices) will be carried out by the two appointed UCI Technical Commissaires, Sandro Coccioni and Alexandre Nouhaud, with the support of Magali Barbe for the check of the jersey at the start area. “Particular attention will be paid to compliance with article 1.3.032 of the UCI regulations, including non-essential elements and clothing or other items/accessories worn by a rider (including but not limited to helmets, glasses, shoes or in-race communication devices) which could modify riders’ morphology.”



Another perspective Milano Cortina 2026 Size does matter: Cheating scandal shows how far athletes will go to pump up gold medal chances However, in practice, there is little enforcement of this rule. The controversy has strong echoes of the “penis-gate” row which erupted at the Winter Olympics earlier this year. That came after three senior members of Norway’s ski jumping staff were banned following a routine equipment check on two Norwegian jumpers after their home world championships in Trondheim. The elastic material around the crotch area was more rigid than officials expected and, once the various layers were opened up, reinforced thread was found woven into the suits, which had also increased the surface area. Accusations of skulduggery peaked with separate claims in German tabloid Bild that some leading ski jumpers had been enlarging their penises by injecting hyaluronic acid.



It is a similar story at the Tour de France Femmes – the nine-day race which is the fifth edition of the women’s event in its current format – with suspicions that some riders are trying to gain an unfair advantage in the time trial by exaggerating their bust size. World.title: High Court overturns reduced sentence for Emma Lovell’s teen killer
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts High Court overturns reduced sentence for Emma Lovell’s teen killer Cloe Read August 5, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The High Court has ruled in favour of the Queensland Attorney-General’s appeal and overturned a killer’s reduced sentence, in one of the state’s most high-profile youth-crime murder cases that contributed to the creation of the “adult crime, adult time” laws. Emma Lovell, a Queensland mother of two, was fatally stabbed in the heart by a 17-year-old boy during a home invasion on Boxing Day 2022. The teenager was sentenced to 14 years behind bars. Emma Lovell died after being stabbed during the home invasion in 2022. Lovell’s death and the attack on their family contributed to the Queensland LNP’s creation of “adult crime, adult time” laws, a central pillar of the party’s promise to crack down on youth crime in the lead-up to the election.



The family had been awoken to their dogs barking, with Lovell’s husband, Lee, opening their bedroom door to discover the teenager in the hallway of their home in North Lakes, north of Brisbane. The parents pushed the teenager, and his co-accused, out of the house, with the attack spilling out onto the front lawn. Lee Lovell repeatedly called for changes to the justice system after his wife was murdered. AAP During the struggle, captured on CCTV, the teenager stabbed Ms Lovell in the chest, and Mr Lovell in the back. Ms Lovell suffered a 13-centimetre knife wound that penetrated her heart. The boy was sentenced in 2024, with 70 per cent of his time to be served behind bars. His offending was deemed “particularly heinous” by the sentencing judge.



However, this was reduced by almost 18 months after an appeal by the teenager. The Queensland Court of Appeal ruled to reduce the sentence on the basis there were special circumstances, including an early guilty plea and the boy’s upbringing. Attorney-General Deb Frecklington was granted leave to appeal that decision, taking the matter to the High Court of Australia. Related Article Courts ‘See it through’: Killer teen’s sentence cut challenged On Thursday, the High Court found it was not open to the Court of Appeal to depart from the sentencing judge’s decision. The High Court said that in his sentencing Justice Tom Sullivan undertook a comprehensive examination of the teenager’s personal circumstances, including parental neglect, violence in the context of excessive consumption of alcohol by adults, and cannabis use by adults.



Sullivan then turned to consider whether there were special circumstances to justify the teenager’s release from detention after serving less than the standard 70 per cent of the period of detention. He ultimately ruled he was not of the view that the teenager’s childhood deprivation, his early plea or his expressions of remorse would be regarded as special circumstances warranting a reduction. “There was nothing about the factors of [the teenager’s] early pleas of guilty, his deprived upbringing, and the positive signs of his ability to rehabilitate that means that it was unreasonable or plainly unjust for the sentencing judge not to reach a conclusion of special circumstances, particularly in light of the seriousness of the offence of murder and the age of the [teenager],” the High Court judgment said. “Indeed, as the sentencing judge observed, the early pleas of guilty by [the teenager] were made against the background of an ‘overwhelmingly strong Crown case’. “And the positive signs of [the teenager’s] ability to rehabilitate were found to show only ‘prospects of being able to be rehabilitated over time’ in circumstances where [the teenager] was found to have, ‘at least to a certain extent’, a lack of ‘willingness to confront the consequences of [his] own actions’.



“The decision in respect of special circumstances tolerated a range of outcomes on the facts.” The High Court ruled that the Attorney-General’s appeal should be allowed, and the orders made by the Court of Appeal should be dismissed. After the High Court hearing earlier this year, Frecklington said the government had listened to Queenslanders, and learned from the tragedy of Lovell’s death to change the laws. “Had this matter happened under our government, this kid would have got life, and that’s the difference,” she said.
