World.title: ‘It was quite traumatic’: Hugo Weaving on overcoming a childhood diagnosis – and the secrets to a happy family
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Hugo Weaving is looking for his turtles. “If we can just get them to put their heads up,” he murmurs, squatting at the edge of his turtle pond and throwing food into the water. “They’re Eastern long-necks,” he explains, “a male and a female. They are definitely a couple, but …” he breaks off. “There’s one! See?!” Two tiny nostrils break the surface of the pond, followed by a pair of perfectly circular bright yellow eyes. It’s like being stared at by an extremely small, extremely suspicious alien. Weaving looks delighted. He’s wearing old trousers and a loose blue jumper, with his grey hair standing out from the back of his head in a wild tangle. “I feel sorry for her,” he confesses, gazing at the turtle. “Every year she wants to lay eggs, and so Harry [Greenwood, his son] and I constructed a big sandbox for her, but there are never any babies. She does lay eggs, but they don’t seem to be viable.” We pause, watching the turtle snap up food in her little muppet mouth. Weaving, 66, is an unusual figure, and not only because of his turtle enthusiasm. He’s much taller and more solidly built in life than he appears on screen, even taller than his official six foot, two inches (188 centimetres); the sort of person you’d notice in a crowd, even if he wasn’t famous. He also has one of those large actor’s heads: big, expressive features, dramatic widow’s peak, exploding hair. The character he most resembles is Elrond, top elf king, whom Weaving has played in three The Lord of the Rings and two The Hobbit movies. Standing in his Sydney kitchen, he is Elrond post-Rivendell, sans jewellery or an elven hairdresser, enjoying his Sauron-free life. Weaving as Elrond in a scene from The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001). Alamy Stock Photo He’s also much friendlier than Elrond would be. During a career spanning more than 40 years, 100-odd films and TV dramas, and dozens of stage productions, Weaving has played every role imaginable. In Australia, he’s most famous for his role in one of our national classics: The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert (which may, Weaving will tell me in due course, at last have a sequel on the way, a mere 32 years after the original). Most recently, he’s added airport chaplain to his CV in the upcoming SBS drama called, yes, The Airport Chaplain. But whatever the character, be it man or machine or drag queen, Weaving’s main claim to fame is his ability – on screen, or on the stage – to project a kind of riveting, enigmatic tension. He’s a master of the cryptic glance, the Delphic silence: you never quite know if he’s about to belt out a disco hit or hurl someone against a dystopian grey wall. All of which makes it a surprise to find him so cheerful in real life. (He’s also kind. A confession: about 10 minutes before the end of this interview, I began to get a migraine. I was too embarrassed to say anything at the time, but when I contacted his agent a few days later and confessed, Weaving immediately agreed to speak on the phone to clarify details I’d missed. This is a kindness he need not have offered, and which filled me with gratitude. Which, in turn, means this story may not be as unbiased as I would otherwise wish. You have been warned.)



Weaving leads me from the front door through to the bright kitchen at the rear of his house. It’s actually two houses: a pair of 19th-century inner-Sydney terraces knocked into one. From the outside, each retains its unrenovated façade: two islands of bohemian life in a sea of investment-banker luxury. Inside, they create exactly the setting in which you’d expect to find an old-school, elder-statesman actor: colourful artworks, vintage furniture, untamed double-width courtyard garden and pool. The turtle pond is right in the middle of the house: a kind of glassed-in light well that illuminates Weaving from behind as he makes mint tea in a battered enamel teapot. “Would you like an Anzac?” he asks. “Kat [Greenwood, Weaving’s partner] made them.” He bustles about, bringing the teapot and a plate of biscuits to the kitchen table. Weaving in his inner-Sydney home, which he shares with longtime partner and former childhood neighbour, Kat Greenwood. Tim Bauer Weaving is an expert in the small joys of domestic life. He had what he describes as a “wonderfully happy childhood” with his parents, older brother and younger sister, moving around the world in the course of his father’s career as a seismologist (and later a computing company executive). He lived first in Nigeria, then England, Melbourne, Sydney and Johannesburg before he turned nine, but did most of his schooling in England. Then, when he was 16, he and his family returned to Sydney permanently, and he’s lived here ever since. “Mum and Dad managed to create this life for all of us,” he says, gesturing with his Anzac, “that combined the stimulation of moving around the world with a strong sense of love and stability inside the family.” Despite this idyllic backstory, Weaving’s parents divorced after he’d finished high school. “I’d actually left home and moved to Woolloomooloo, he recalls. “So I wasn’t damaged by it in the sense I might have been if I was 11 or 12. But it was very, very difficult for my mum and dad, and difficult for the whole family. And I was grateful that I was able, to some extent, to deal with it as a semi-adult.” Weaving was accepted directly (and unusually) into the National Institute of Dramatic Art from school. After finishing his NIDA training, he was immediately offered a two-year contract with the Sydney Theatre Company, alongside Mel Gibson and Judy Davis, Colin Friels and Ruth Cracknell. At 24, he starred in his first TV series, the 1984 smash hit Bodyline, and endeared himself to Australians everywhere by playing exactly the kind of supercilious, upper-class English villain (Test cricket captain Douglas Jardine) we most love to hate. More iconic roles followed – not overnight, but with reliable steadiness: Proof (Jocelyn Moorhouse’s 1991 low-budget gem); Priscilla in 1994; and then two Hollywood blockbuster trilogies: The Matrix from 1999; and The Lord of the Rings from 2001.



During this period, he also managed to fall in love with artist (and master Anzac biscuit maker) Greenwood and have two children, Harry (an actor, 37) and Holly (an artist, 34) Greenwood. These days, Weaving divides his time between roles in Australia and abroad (London, Ireland and New Zealand in the past couple of years), life in Sydney (he’s a passionate Sydney Swans supporter) and trips to the family property in the NSW Hunter region (where he plants gum trees and, presumably, consumes an infinite number of excellent homemade biscuits and cups of mint tea). With Cate Blanchett in Little Fish (2005). Sitting opposite him at his wide wooden table in his warm, sunlit kitchen, I’m reminded of a phrase he used years ago, in the brilliant Australian film Little Fish. Weaving plays Lionel, the father of Cate Blanchett’s Tracy, whom he calls his “shiny, shiny girl”. And at least on first impressions, this phrase seems appropriate to the scene before me now. Hugo Weaving looks like a man with a shiny, shiny life. Is it just me, or is The Airport Chaplain a terrible name for a TV show? Still, at least you know what you’re getting. Weaving plays Tobias Wallace, a kindly but enigmatic (surprise!) multi-faith-friendly fixer at Melbourne International Airport. Wallace’s average day is spent dealing with everything from dead bodies to dog poo while helping people through the most horrendously stressful drama life has to offer: attempting to board a plane. Meanwhile, of course, it’s clear he has his own horrendously stressful life drama brewing behind the scenes. Do airport chaplains actually exist? “Yes!” exclaims Weaving, leaning forward. “Do you know Jude Troy? She’s the producer. She was at Melbourne airport, and she … did she lose her passport? There was some issue like that – something quite dramatic.” In fact, Troy left her bag – with all her ID, her computer, her phone – in the back of an Uber at the airport. “Oh my god,” she says, recalling the incident. “I remember standing at the Qantas desk, totally frantic, and they introduced me to this man with ‘chaplain’ on his vest. And I was like, ‘I do not need a priest!’ ” And yet, “a few hours later I was on a flight home, bags beside me, upgraded – all thanks to this wonderful man.” No wonder she co-created and produced a TV series based on him.



Working with Weaving, Troy says, was “an honour. I know everyone says that. But he could do the role – any role, really – with his eyes closed, and yet he gave it such care and diligence. He interrogated every line, every setting, every costume – right down to how many lanyards he should wear.” “I do have this childlike interest in dress-ups,” admits Weaving: “in imaginary games, playing. But what that is, actually, is trying to put yourself in another place, transport yourself inside another human being. It’s a way of understanding the other.” This is what he’s always loved about acting. “Once I tapped into what that creative journey of acting might entail, I think I was really, really interested in it.” His preparation for roles is famously immersive. “It doesn’t always look like it’s a joy,” confessed old friend and fellow actor Richard Roxburgh recently. “I’m just aware there’s a price that he’s paying in there.” Weaving grins. “Rox is such a wonderful actor; he just wants to be in the place and play. And I do, too, but I can’t play if I don’t understand. So I will read every book, consult every source I can find.” As an actor, Weaving says, “you can’t let [your character] off the hook … but it’s not up to you to judge. It’s up to you to inhabit.” Tim Bauer This gives his characterisations real richness, say colleagues. Paula Arundell, a close friend and collaborator for more than 20 years, first saw Weaving perform in Sydney in 1995. “My first thought was ‘He’s so tall!’ ” She laughs. “And he’s so full – full and present on stage. It’s like he can gather all the little pixellations of a character and shimmeringly put them together, so you’re witnessing the full vibration of a real human being on stage in front of you – not just an outline.” “He’s always percolating,” agrees Heather Mitchell, who’s known him since they were both at NIDA in the late 1970s. “He’s never just listening and responding. He’s sharing an idea – a whole world – with you. And that makes you a better actor, because he sort of endows you with sincerity: he believes in you, he believes in the moment.”



One wonders, then, what he believes when he’s playing an objectively terrible person. In 2018, Weaving starred in Patrick Melrose, a fictionalised true story about writer Teddy St Aubyn, who was raped by his own father as a child. Weaving played this father, David Melrose. Does a role like this impinge on his own peace of mind? Weaving looks surprised. “No, not at all. It doesn’t stay with me.” He stops, thinking. “As an actor, you’re trying to embody not just the illness – this hideous, misogynist and abusive paedophile – but the human. You can’t let them off the hook, you can’t sentimentalise. But at the same time, it’s not up to you to judge. It’s up to you to inhabit. But it doesn’t mean you can’t be on set and then when it’s ‘cut’, you can’t have a laugh as Hugo. Because actually it was a very joyful set.” Weaving portraying a “hideous, misogynist and abusive paedophile” in the 2018 TV series, Patrick Melrose. Weaving loves the collegiate creativity of sets and rehearsal rooms. Back in 2012, he was – unusually for him – critical about his part in three of the four animated Transformer movies, in which he had a voice-over role as arch-villain Megatron. His ire seemed mostly self-directed: he confessed he’d never met director Michael Bay in person or read the script, and that he found his role “meaningless”. “Very rarely have I said I’d do something and I wasn’t really interested in it,” he says now. “Transformers was an example. I said no to it three times, [then] eventually I did it. But when you do make choices like that, you end up …” He pauses. “It doesn’t have the same meaning. So everything I do is something that excites me.” “He wants the work to be good. And he wants to be good,” says playwright Angus Cerini, who wrote Wonnangatta, in which Hugo starred in 2020. “He interrogates, but with real kindness.” “He has a kind of gentle command,” is how Mitchell puts it. “He thinks so deeply, not just about his role, but the whole story. He’s never forceful and never selfish, but he’s very decisive. I’ve been working with him when he’s said, ‘No, I really believe this is the way it must be. This is how I see it.’ If something’s truthful for him, he will stand by it.” Despite his success, and his dedication, you could argue acting is a strange career for Hugo Weaving. He describes himself as a “very shy, very shy little boy. Because we moved so much, I just had to experience the new place, the new school, the new house. And it was wonderful, and my eyes were continually opened. But I was also aware that I always felt like the ground underneath my feet was shifting.”

World.title: Beautiful, brilliant and forgotten: The music star who inspired Vivaldi
World.content:
The composer wrote some of his most challenging work for Anna Maria della Pieta. Violinist Augusta McKay Lodge says it’s like “a tightrope walk on strings”.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It seems only a matter of time before the story of Anna Maria della Pieta, the prodigious violinist who inspired Vivaldi, is turned into a movie. The opening scene might show a newborn being dropped off at Venice’s Ospedale della Pieta, a home for unwanted infants where the girls were trained as musicians and performed sacred music that drew audiences from across Europe. Under the cover of darkness, Anna Maria is placed in the scafetta, an opening in the ospedale’s wall. Her mother rings a bell and walks away. It’s a harsh start to life, but preferable to being drowned in a canal, the fate of many of the city’s illegitimate babies in the 18th century. Fast forward eight years and we find Anna Maria playing for the ospedale’s violin tutor Antonio Vivaldi, a red-haired Catholic priest. There are many fine musicians in Pieta’s all-female orchestra and choir – an ensemble that played, for modesty’s sake, behind metal grilles in raised galleries – but it is clear that Anna Maria is exceptional. Vivaldi procures instruments worthy of her talent and begins to write music that showcases her technical ability. An anonymous poet declares that when she played her violin “countless angels dare to hover near”. Anna Maria, opined a French scholar, was on a par with, or perhaps even better than, the masterful Italian violinist Giuseppe Tartini. Micky White, a Venice-based British researcher and the author of Antonio Vivaldi: A Life in Documents, says there is evidence to support the rave reviews. “She was an extraordinary musician who didn’t only play the violin, but other instruments such as the viola d’amore, mandolin, theorbo [a 14-string lute] and harpsichord,” she says. “These other instruments were not secondary; she was a virtuoso on all of them. She could play anything he [Vivaldi] could write for her.” Evidence of the creative relationship between the tutor and his star pupil can be found in Anna Maria’s “part book”, a red leather-bound collection of her personal repertoire now held in the library of Venice conservatory. It contains the violin parts to 26 concertos Vivaldi wrote for her; an extraordinary testament to her ability and the faith the composer of The Four Seasons placed in it. Some of that repertoire – notably the violin concerto in E major “per Anna Maria” as well as work written for her by Tartini and Pisendel – will be performed by the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra (ABO) in a recital designed to shine a spotlight on a woman who was a star in her lifetime, but relegated to a footnote by Vivaldi’s resurgence in the early part of the 20th century.



Augusta McKay Lodge, an American violinist living in Paris, will make her Australian debut as soloist and guest director and Anna Maria’s story will be narrated by NIDA graduate Lilian Alejandra Valverde from a script written by Alana Valentine. Poppy Townsend, another young NIDA graduate, has designed the lighting. Augusta McKay Lodge says the music Vivaldi wrote for Anna Maria is testament to her skill: “It’s like a tightrope walk on the strings with nothing underneath.″⁣ Lauren Desberg Related Article Sigrid Thornton Sigrid Thornton is about to play a matchmaker. This time, it’s sure to work The ABO’s co-founder and artistic director, Paul Dyer, said it was a deliberate choice to get young talent to tell Anna Maria’s story. “I sat them down and said ‘I’ve got a gift for you’,” he recalls. “It’s the story of a young woman who lived 300 years ago and has only come into the public eye in the past 15 years or so. She was abandoned, she doesn’t have a surname and she lived with all these other girls in a place where there was just one man: a red-haired priest. I said I want this story to be factual, but I want to bring it into the 21st century.” The Anna Maria revival that Dyer alludes to began, perhaps, with the rather breathlessly titled Vivaldi’s Virgins, an historical novel by Barbara Quick published in 2007. More recently, The Instrumentalist, a 2024 novel by Harriet Constable, imagines the relationship between Anna Maria and Vivaldi as a battle of wills that becomes increasingly acrimonious as the composer takes credit for his protégé’s work. Michele Riondino as Vivaldi and Tecla Insolia as Cecilia in Primavera. Meanwhile, Primavera, the debut feature of Italian director Damiano Michieletto, has Vivaldi tutoring Cecilia, a young orphan violinist who “channels” the spirit of Anna Maria. The film had its premiere at the Toronto Film Festival last year.



Anna Maria’s story lends itself to fiction because, despite her celebrity, she is something of an enigma. True, there are documents revealing details of her long life (she was 86 when she died at the Pieta on August 10, 1782), but they mostly focus on things like the purchase of her instruments or her rapid rise through the ranks (she was appointed maestra di violino and maestra di coro at the remarkably young age of 42). A 1686 engraving of the Ospedale della Pieta in Venice. De Agostini via Getty Images Sadly, there are no portraits, so we have to take the word of a poet that she was blonde, beautiful and had a “snow-white breast”. Her inner life, her thoughts about her abandonment, her relationship with Vivaldi and the reason she never left the Ospedale della Pieta despite being free to do so if she married, are unknown and open to speculation. McKay Lodge says she is reading The Instrumentalist “for fun” as she prepares for the ABO concerts. The novel “brings Anna Maria to life in a way that’s kind of hard for us to imagine just listening to the music,” she says. Related Article New music A hero to Harry Styles and Frank Ocean, the Durutti Column’s Vini Reilly is back from the brink Asked about the book’s suggestion that Vivaldi may have appropriated Anna Maria’s work, she says, “That’s only speculation. But at that time people were ‘stealing’ from each other all the time and recycling their own themes in new works. Handel is infamous for that. There was no copyright back then.” What is really unfortunate, says McKay Lodge, is the fact that none of Anna Maria’s compositions survived. “She probably was a very prolific composer and we’ll never know the extent of it.” The “extremely virtuosic” nature of Vivaldi’s compositions are a testament to Anna Maria’s ability, says McKay Lodge. Some passages include notes so high that violinists have to venture beyond the fingerboard of the instrument. “It’s like a tightrope walk on the strings with nothing underneath,” she says. Likewise, the inclusion of “big double stops”, a challenging technique where notes are played simultaneously on different strings, could also be interpreted as evidence of her technical excellence.

World.title: ‘We need to densify’: Why the 15-minute city could be the key to Melbourne’s housing crisis
World.content:
Carlos Moreno, the15-minute city pioneer, will be a keynote speaker at Melbourne Assembly, a conference The Age is hosting in October to share ideas shaping the future of our city.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Carlos Moreno is used to defending the idea of a 15-minute city. His radical idea of bringing work, schools and essential services within a short walk of every resident has been widely adopted around the world, but it has also been weaponised by online agitators as a blueprint for government surveillance and criticised for embedding inequality. The French academic is undeterred and believes it might just be the essential, urgent prescription needed to fix Melbourne’s housing crisis. Carlos Moreno is the man behind the idea of 15-minute cities. Moreno developed the concept a decade ago as a means to a low-traffic, low-carbon future, but he says it is as relevant as ever as a way to address housing affordability and make Melbourne’s fringes more liveable. “People pushed into living far away have difficulty accessing the local services, medical services, cultural activities and educational services,” he says over a video call early in the morning from Paris, where he lives. “For this reason the 15-minute city is an amazing opportunity for transforming radically this situation.” Moreno and former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio are two of the keynote speakers at The Age’s upcoming Melbourne Assembly, which will be held in October.



Melbourne Assembly will bring together some of the world’s brightest minds across city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for Melbourne’s future. What is a 15-minute city? Moreno, who teaches at the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, coined the phrase “15-minute city” in 2016, and it was embraced by a group of nearly 100 mayors worldwide as a way to help recover from the COVID pandemic. A 15-minute city is a principle that everything you need should be within 15 minutes’ walk of your home – schools, shops, libraries, parks, transport, job opportunities and healthcare. The idea is that a network of 15-minute cities provides inhabitants with easy access to everything they need. If you live in a city, how long does it take you to get to a supermarket? What about a pharmacy or a school? For adherents of the 15-minute-city concept, the answer to all those questions should be “less than 15 minutes” – and it should not involve a car journey. The actual timeframe is slightly fluid: 15-minute cities are also referred to in urban planning speak as 20-minute neighbourhoods, and Copenhagen trumped everyone with a “Five Minutes to Everything” model.



The concept has provided inspiration to the City of Melbourne and the Victorian government, which implemented “20-minute neighbourhoods” in its statewide planning and development strategy Plan Victoria. “We have a global movement for implementing this idea, reducing the role of individual cars, preserving biodiversity, developing a more vibrant local economy and developing a new economical geography,” Moreno says. Related Article Note From The Editor They sought Melbourne’s Opera House and found something much better. It all started with a conversation Moreno says the lack of affordable housing near services, jobs and retail hubs makes the need to shift to 15-minute cities even more urgent. “The housing crisis is not only in the Victorian state, the question of the housing crisis is a worldwide crisis,” Moreno says. Melbourne’s urban challenge Moreno devotes a chapter of his book The 15-Minute City: A Solution To Saving Our Time And Our Planet to Melbourne, referring approvingly to it as a “pioneering” 20-minute city.



However, even Moreno concedes Melbourne’s sprawling suburbs and large “McMansions” are a barrier to creating walkable neighbourhoods. He says a mindset shift is needed to move from focusing on the importance of individual homes to prioritising sociability instead with higher-density living. He wants to see more apartments where residents spend more time out and about at libraries, local shops, cinemas and theatres instead of in cars commuting to their jobs from large homes in the outer suburbs. “We need to develop this new kind of social infrastructure for offering these new kind of services,” Moreno says. “This is today one of the rules for transforming our cities. We need to densify because the presence of the massive individual homes represent a relevant cost for us collectively.” Moreno points to the high infrastructure cost of building in greenfield outer suburbs where roads, public transport, sewerage and power all need to be installed. It’s an argument the Victorian government has deployed in designating 60 activity centres across Melbourne – including areas such as Camberwell, Brighton, Ringwood and Frankston – where it is seizing local planning controls.



Related Article Planning The inner Melbourne suburbs set for high-density housing revealed In these zones, the government controversially allows developers to bypass local councils to build high-density apartments up to 20 storeys. Moreno says he supports more development around transport links such as train stations because it helps reduce car dependency, which causes traffic jams, contributes to pollution and reduces physical activity. “We need to transform these places, we need to densify,” he says. “Low densification was the lifestyle of the 20th century, this is no longer possible in the 21st century.” Conspiracy theories and death threats Moreno’s work has attracted opposition including from what he calls “conspiracy mongers” who are concerned that 15-minute cities are really designed to restrict people’s movements so they can be better surveilled by the government. Some claim 15-minute cities represent the first step to open-air jails where residents will not be allowed to leave their prescribed area.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Cross-examination continues of complainant on third day of alleged indecent assault, sexual touching trial
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the third day of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. Our reporters Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

This week, the NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court complex has heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing when the man was a teenager in year 12 in the early 2000s. Jones denies the claims.

Alan Jones arrives at the Downing Centre Local Court in Sydney on Wednesday. Audrey Richardson

The man, now in his early 40s, gave evidence that Jones also groped him as he drove the then-radio host to his Fitzroy Falls farm. On Tuesday, “J” told the court that Jones had indecently assaulted him at the property after telling him to wear “a robe and nothing else”.

The complainant said he came forward to police after seeing reports about Jones’ arrest in November 2024 because he wanted justice.

“I just want justice for what happened; that’s why I’m here,” he said. “I’m here because it’s the right thing to do and people need me, people need me to do this.”

Jones had supported the promising athlete financially, including paying him hundreds of dollars a week to focus on training and giving him a car and a mobile phone, the court heard.

Today, the man known as complainant “J” returns to the witness box. He will face further cross-examination by Jones’ barrister Gabrielle Bashir, SC, which started on Tuesday afternoon.

Bashir has asked “J” a series of questions about whether he read media reports containing similar allegations about Jones in 2023 before he spoke to police the following year. He said he did not.

The Crown alleges Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men between 2003 and 2020 and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him, including nine indecent assault charges against “J”.

The former broadcaster has emphatically denied wrongdoing and Bashir said on Monday that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

“Rivalry, treachery, double-dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more are all at the heart of this case,” Bashir said in her opening remarks to Judge Glenn Walsh.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: What HSC economics students ask Ross Gittins the most
World.content:
NationalNSWHSC What HSC economics students ask Ross Gittins the most Emily Kowal August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At the end of every year, like clockwork, Ross Gittins’ inbox fills with the same request, sent by a year 12 economics student: Could he please post them a signed photo of himself? Their teacher is a big fan. “I am the rock star of high school economics. It is absurd,” Gittins laughs. For five decades, economics students have turned to The Sydney Morning Herald economics editor’s columns to prepare for their exams and assignments. Now, they have had the chance to ask Gittins, and his protégée, economics writer Millie Muroi, their economics questions as they prepare for their trials and final exams. The questions were varied and broad. Riley Hughes from Cranbrook School asked how the government should balance taxes on cigarettes given the illicit tobacco black market, while Layne Phillips from Pymble Ladies’ College asked Gittins and Muroi how young people should deal with exorbitant house prices.



“Is it important that we stay optimistic and continue working within the system, or is the level of housing affordability and inaccessibility a reason for us to be more critical and push for change?” Layne asked. In response, Gittins said young people should “stay within the system” but fight for change. “The system has been allowed to run in a way that gives a lot of benefit to people who already own a home. It’s wonderful for me, but it’s not wonderful for some young person who might want to buy my house,” said Gittins. “The risk we have with this is we have a generation of young people who say the system is biased against us, we are going to put up a fight against the system. It’s your system as much as it is all the oldies’. What we need to do is change that system so that it gives everybody, particularly young people, a better deal.”



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy Your boss will hate this economic fix … but you’ll love it Ross Gittins Economics Editor Emily Wu from Hornsby Girls High asked whether we should change the way we measure the health of Australia’s labour market. “As AI and automation begin to replace labour, do you believe we should put more emphasis on labour under-utilisation data to better understand the true capacity of the Australian workforce?” Wu asked. Amid declining enrolments in HSC economics, Gittins praised the subject. “The great strength of high school economics is that it’s so closely based on current events,” he said.



“When you actually study it, rather than think about studying it, you find out it’s quite interesting, and it gets you engaged in the political process in a way that most HSC subjects don’t.” Check out everything students asked Gittins and Muroi here. Ross Gittins unpacks the economy in an exclusive subscriber-only newsletter. Sign up to receive it every Tuesday evening.

World.title: Jenolan Caves is set to reopen. But getting there is going to be tricky
World.content:
NationalNSWCity life Jenolan Caves is set to reopen. But getting there is going to be tricky Julie Power August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW’s Jenolan Caves is scheduled to reopen early next year, after six years of natural disasters that caused catastrophic damage to access roads, the precinct and the historic mountain retreat Caves House. But long-term access to the site has yet to be finalised, and it is unlikely that vehicles will be allowed into the precinct again, or to enter via the Grand Arch, as they did for decades. Jenolan Caves Reserve Trust director Andrew Le Lievre hopes the public can return, even though the roads may never reopen. Wolter Peeters Before Jenolan reopens, the state government is expected to consider a range of alternate transport options including a $44 million detachable gondola, a cable car similar to the one used at Taronga Zoo in Sydney. It would transport visitors from the escarpment to the valley through 1154 metres. Jenolan Caves Reserve Trust director Andrew Le Lievre said he was working with Transport for NSW on providing a fleet of shuttle buses that could carry hundreds of visitors from a parking lot at the top of the hill.



“Our preferred option is not to have the public driving on that road. It is very steep, it is very narrow and it’s very windy,” he said. The member for Bathurst Paul Toole said a gondola from the Two Mile Road section of Jenolan Caves Road to Caves House was a “no-brainer solution” that would resolve financial and geographical issues. “A gondola will add to the magical experience of Jenolan Caves and offer a new perspective as visitors glide down the valley,” Toole said. The cost and reliability of the gondola was the preferred option in a report by consultants Riser + Gain. It was the most cost-effective and the least damaging for biodiversity and the limestone. The report estimated that it would cost at least $150 million to fix the Five Mile section of Jenolan Caves Road. Even then it would still be vulnerable to land slips. It is still closed and Transport for NSW is expected to make a final decision on the viability of future repairs in the next few months.



Repairs to the Two Mile section of Jenolan Caves Road were estimated at more than $57 million and are expected to be completed this year, depending on weather. In future it will serve as an access road. Related Article Roads ‘Mind-blowing’: How a convict-built crossing closed a Blue Mountains highway Victoria Pass is also currently closed on the Great Western Highway between Mount Victoria and Little Hartley, causing further delays for visitors from Sydney and the Blue Mountains. Following upgrades and restoration works across the site, Le Lievre said visitors would be able to visit caves that hadn’t been open to the public for years. These include: the Ribbon, famous for its gravity-defying helictites; the Jubilee, with its rich crystal displays; and the River Cave, described as a “mind-bending labyrinth”. Guides would escort visitors to give them a sense of wonder and awe that came with discovering something new to them yet older than 340 million years.



Le Lievre said: “One of our major challenges has been that people have been to the caves usually as schoolchildren and they feel that that’s the experience, only to come back with potentially children or grandchildren.” Paul Toole, member for Bathurst, visting Jenolan Caves. Paul Toole MP Toole said the reopening of Jenolan Caves would provide a significant boost to local businesses, jobs and the wider regional economy. It was one of the region’s “greatest natural treasures for generations, drawing visitors from across Australia and around the world”. The oldest open cave system in the world also has a new attraction: a chance for the public to spot one of the world’s latest discoveries, a cave cricket about the size of a coffee bean. Known as the Jenolan Cave Cricket, it is called the Speleotettix binoomea, a reference to the traditional Indigenous name for Jenolan that means dark spaces. It is the first time a word used by the traditional Gundungurra people has been used to describe a species.



Researchers have recently described a new species of cave cricket, found within the cave systems of Jenolan, Wombeyan and Abercrombie. Dr Anne Musser Environment Minister Penny Sharpe said the cricket’s discovery was “a powerful reminder of the area’s unique natural and cultural significance”. After the pandemic the caves attracted fewer than 50,000 visitors a year, compared with 240,000 a year, on average, before then. After assessing other options, including a funicular, the report recommended a mono-detachable gondola that could transport about 900 visitors per hour per direction (1800 in total), or about 500,000 a year in the short term and more if needed later. The absence of vehicles for six years from the site, combined with National Parks’ work to remove feral animals, had helped re-establish brushed tail possums, which were on the brink of extinction in 1988. Other native animals had flourished, including the spotted-tailed quoll and a family of three platypus in the Blue Lake.

World.title: Cyclists accused of ‘faking larger bra size’ at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
SportTour de France Cyclists accused of ‘faking larger bra size’ at Tour de France Femmes Tom Cary and Jeremy Wilson August 5, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A row has broken out at the Tour de France Femmes following allegations some riders are artificially exaggerating their bust size to gain a “bra booster” aerodynamic advantage for the time trial. Riders were checked before the fourth stage of the Tour on Tuesday by officials to ensure they were not wearing padded bras or hiding other objects between their chest and clothing. At least one rider was seen being checked pre-stage by a male official, accompanied by a female witness. The peloton passes through the village of Chexbres during the second stage of the women’s Tour de France. AP According to WielerFlits, a leading cycling news platform in the Netherlands and Belgium, “several” women’s WorldTour teams have raised concerns riders are padding their bras to “fake” a larger cup size. How does ‘bra boosting’ work?



Referred to as “chest fairing”, increasing the surface area of the chest can change the airflow around the cyclist during the time trial and create a measurable benefit over multiple kilometres. Bert Blocken, professor of aerodynamics at Heriot-Watt University in Scotland and LUT in Finland, who has produced studies on the subject, said he had been sent photographs that “seemed to suggest that there are indeed some objects that some female riders stick behind their shirt”. Blocken added that “it was definitely a concern with the men’s races in 2023 and 2024”, which was then addressed in a scientific article he had published. Blocken said he had also talked to the International Cycling Union (UCI), the world governing body for the sport, about the issues. Titled “Analysis of chest fairings in time trial cycling” the scientific review found chest fairing can give a 3.6 per cent drag reduction and concluded that “time gains by chest fairing can decide who wins or loses a time trial”.



Blocken’s article defines chest-fairing as when “some cyclists in triathlon and road cycling competitions have been riding with an object stuck between their chest and their shirt, attempting to reduce aerodynamic drag”. The most excessive examples had previously occurred in triathlon, with the use of water bottles. Blocken wrote that “cyclists, cycling teams and cycling product manufacturers are constantly looking for aerodynamic improvements that can withstand the scrutiny of the UCI”. Blocken stressed that he does not follow women’s cycling closely but said he had been shown the photographs by a journalist from WielerFlits. Both the UCI and the Tour de France Femmes were approached for comment before Tuesday’s time trial. The teams WielerFlits spoke to anonymously believe the UCI should have a female official check the riders immediately after the time trial in a closed tent to ensure they are not concealing anything in their bra or under their aero clothing.



Why would a larger bust help in time trialling? It might sound counterintuitive that a “larger” skinsuit would help to produce an aerodynamic advantage. Would not wrinkles or loose, baggy fabric slow a rider down? Well, yes they would. But the theory behind artificially inflating your bust is that by altering the shape of the chest, a rider can create a better airflow underneath a perfectly tight skinsuit. In time trials, riders adopt a tucked position with their forearms close together over their bars. This creates a pocket or “valley” between the helmet, shoulders and chest. Air flowing into that depression can separate and become turbulent, increasing drag. Netherlands’ Lorena Wiebes of team SD Worx Protime, centre, crosses the finish line to win the second stage of the women’s tour from Aigle to Geneva. AP By adding carefully shaped padding to the chest, the front of the rider becomes rounder and smoother, guiding the airflow cleanly around the body.



Blocken’s thesis, published on ScienceDirect two years ago, concluded that riders could achieve a reduction in air resistance of up to 3.6 per cent when using an object in the optimal shape that covers the chest. This translates into a time saving of at least 0.78 seconds per kilometre. Why is “chest fairing” controversial? Artificially altering clothing is prohibited by the (UCI). If a rider is caught during or after a race and in violation of UCI’s regulations, they could face immediate disqualification and fined. Before Tuesday’s time trial, race organisers announced they would attempt to prevent any scandal from arising by requiring riders to report for bike and outfit checks at least 10 minutes before the start of the fourth stage. In their stage three jury report, organisers added: “Pre-checks on riders’ equipment (race and spare bikes, their respective accessories and devices) will be carried out by the two appointed UCI Technical Commissaires, Sandro Coccioni and Alexandre Nouhaud, with the support of Magali Barbe for the check of the jersey at the start area. “Particular attention will be paid to compliance with article 1.3.032 of the UCI regulations, including non-essential elements and clothing or other items/accessories worn by a rider (including but not limited to helmets, glasses, shoes or in-race communication devices) which could modify riders’ morphology.”



Another perspective Milano Cortina 2026 Size does matter: Cheating scandal shows how far athletes will go to pump up gold medal chances However, in practice, there is little enforcement of this rule. The controversy has strong echoes of the “penis-gate” row which erupted at the Winter Olympics earlier this year. That came after three senior members of Norway’s ski jumping staff were banned following a routine equipment check on two Norwegian jumpers after their home world championships in Trondheim. The elastic material around the crotch area was more rigid than officials expected and, once the various layers were opened up, reinforced thread was found woven into the suits, which had also increased the surface area. Accusations of skulduggery peaked with separate claims in German tabloid Bild that some leading ski jumpers had been enlarging their penises by injecting hyaluronic acid.



It is a similar story at the Tour de France Femmes – the nine-day race which is the fifth edition of the women’s event in its current format – with suspicions that some riders are trying to gain an unfair advantage in the time trial by exaggerating their bust size. The Telegraph, London News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: High Court overturns reduced sentence for Emma Lovell’s teen killer
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts High Court overturns reduced sentence for Emma Lovell’s teen killer Cloe Read August 5, 2026 — 11:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The High Court has ruled in favour of the Queensland Attorney-General’s appeal and overturned a killer’s reduced sentence, in one of the state’s most high-profile youth-crime murder cases that contributed to the creation of the “adult crime, adult time” laws. Emma Lovell, a Queensland mother of two, was fatally stabbed in the heart by a 17-year-old boy during a home invasion on Boxing Day 2022. The teenager was sentenced to 14 years behind bars. Emma Lovell died after being stabbed during the home invasion in 2022. Lovell’s death and the attack on their family contributed to the Queensland LNP’s creation of “adult crime, adult time” laws, a central pillar of the party’s promise to crack down on youth crime in the lead-up to the election.



The family had been awoken to their dogs barking, with Lovell’s husband, Lee, opening their bedroom door to discover the teenager in the hallway of their home in North Lakes, north of Brisbane. The parents pushed the teenager, and his co-accused, out of the house, with the attack spilling out onto the front lawn. Lee Lovell repeatedly called for changes to the justice system after his wife was murdered. AAP During the struggle, captured on CCTV, the teenager stabbed Ms Lovell in the chest, and Mr Lovell in the back. Ms Lovell suffered a 13-centimetre knife wound that penetrated her heart. The boy was sentenced in 2024, with 70 per cent of his time to be served behind bars. His offending was deemed “particularly heinous” by the sentencing judge.



However, this was reduced by almost 18 months after an appeal by the teenager. The Queensland Court of Appeal ruled to reduce the sentence on the basis there were special circumstances, including an early guilty plea and the boy’s upbringing. Attorney-General Deb Frecklington was granted leave to appeal that decision, taking the matter to the High Court of Australia. Related Article Courts ‘See it through’: Killer teen’s sentence cut challenged On Thursday, the High Court found it was not open to the Court of Appeal to depart from the sentencing judge’s decision. The High Court said that in his sentencing Justice Tom Sullivan undertook a comprehensive examination of the teenager’s personal circumstances, including parental neglect, violence in the context of excessive consumption of alcohol by adults, and cannabis use by adults.



Sullivan then turned to consider whether there were special circumstances to justify the teenager’s release from detention after serving less than the standard 70 per cent of the period of detention. He ultimately ruled he was not of the view that the teenager’s childhood deprivation, his early plea or his expressions of remorse would be regarded as special circumstances warranting a reduction. “There was nothing about the factors of [the teenager’s] early pleas of guilty, his deprived upbringing, and the positive signs of his ability to rehabilitate that means that it was unreasonable or plainly unjust for the sentencing judge not to reach a conclusion of special circumstances, particularly in light of the seriousness of the offence of murder and the age of the [teenager],” the High Court judgment said. “Indeed, as the sentencing judge observed, the early pleas of guilty by [the teenager] were made against the background of an ‘overwhelmingly strong Crown case’. “And the positive signs of [the teenager’s] ability to rehabilitate were found to show only ‘prospects of being able to be rehabilitated over time’ in circumstances where [the teenager] was found to have, ‘at least to a certain extent’, a lack of ‘willingness to confront the consequences of [his] own actions’.



“The decision in respect of special circumstances tolerated a range of outcomes on the facts.” The High Court ruled that the Attorney-General’s appeal should be allowed, and the orders made by the Court of Appeal should be dismissed. After the High Court hearing earlier this year, Frecklington said the government had listened to Queenslanders, and learned from the tragedy of Lovell’s death to change the laws. “Had this matter happened under our government, this kid would have got life, and that’s the difference,” she said. World.title: ‘It was quite traumatic’: Hugo Weaving on overcoming a childhood diagnosis – and the secrets to a happy family
World.content:

Hugo Weaving is looking for his turtles. “If we can just get them to put their heads up,” he murmurs, squatting at the edge of his turtle pond and throwing food into the water. “They’re Eastern long-necks,” he explains, “a male and a female. They are definitely a couple, but …” he breaks off. “There’s one! See?!” Two tiny nostrils break the surface of the pond, followed by a pair of perfectly circular bright yellow eyes. It’s like being stared at by an extremely small, extremely suspicious alien. Weaving looks delighted. He’s wearing old trousers and a loose blue jumper, with his grey hair standing out from the back of his head in a wild tangle. “I feel sorry for her,” he confesses, gazing at the turtle. “Every year she wants to lay eggs, and so Harry [Greenwood, his son] and I constructed a big sandbox for her, but there are never any babies. She does lay eggs, but they don’t seem to be viable.” We pause, watching the turtle snap up food in her little muppet mouth. Weaving, 66, is an unusual figure, and not only because of his turtle enthusiasm. He’s much taller and more solidly built in life than he appears on screen, even taller than his official six foot, two inches (188 centimetres); the sort of person you’d notice in a crowd, even if he wasn’t famous. He also has one of those large actor’s heads: big, expressive features, dramatic widow’s peak, exploding hair. The character he most resembles is Elrond, top elf king, whom Weaving has played in three The Lord of the Rings and two The Hobbit movies. Standing in his Sydney kitchen, he is Elrond post-Rivendell, sans jewellery or an elven hairdresser, enjoying his Sauron-free life. Weaving as Elrond in a scene from The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001). Alamy Stock Photo He’s also much friendlier than Elrond would be. During a career spanning more than 40 years, 100-odd films and TV dramas, and dozens of stage productions, Weaving has played every role imaginable. In Australia, he’s most famous for his role in one of our national classics: The Adventures of Priscilla, Queen of the Desert (which may, Weaving will tell me in due course, at last have a sequel on the way, a mere 32 years after the original). Most recently, he’s added airport chaplain to his CV in the upcoming SBS drama called, yes, The Airport Chaplain. But whatever the character, be it man or machine or drag queen, Weaving’s main claim to fame is his ability – on screen, or on the stage – to project a kind of riveting, enigmatic tension. He’s a master of the cryptic glance, the Delphic silence: you never quite know if he’s about to belt out a disco hit or hurl someone against a dystopian grey wall. All of which makes it a surprise to find him so cheerful in real life. (He’s also kind. A confession: about 10 minutes before the end of this interview, I began to get a migraine. I was too embarrassed to say anything at the time, but when I contacted his agent a few days later and confessed, Weaving immediately agreed to speak on the phone to clarify details I’d missed. This is a kindness he need not have offered, and which filled me with gratitude. Which, in turn, means this story may not be as unbiased as I would otherwise wish. You have been warned.)



Weaving leads me from the front door through to the bright kitchen at the rear of his house. It’s actually two houses: a pair of 19th-century inner-Sydney terraces knocked into one. From the outside, each retains its unrenovated façade: two islands of bohemian life in a sea of investment-banker luxury. Inside, they create exactly the setting in which you’d expect to find an old-school, elder-statesman actor: colourful artworks, vintage furniture, untamed double-width courtyard garden and pool. The turtle pond is right in the middle of the house: a kind of glassed-in light well that illuminates Weaving from behind as he makes mint tea in a battered enamel teapot. “Would you like an Anzac?” he asks. “Kat [Greenwood, Weaving’s partner] made them.” He bustles about, bringing the teapot and a plate of biscuits to the kitchen table. Weaving in his inner-Sydney home, which he shares with longtime partner and former childhood neighbour, Kat Greenwood. Tim Bauer Weaving is an expert in the small joys of domestic life. He had what he describes as a “wonderfully happy childhood” with his parents, older brother and younger sister, moving around the world in the course of his father’s career as a seismologist (and later a computing company executive). He lived first in Nigeria, then England, Melbourne, Sydney and Johannesburg before he turned nine, but did most of his schooling in England. Then, when he was 16, he and his family returned to Sydney permanently, and he’s lived here ever since. “Mum and Dad managed to create this life for all of us,” he says, gesturing with his Anzac, “that combined the stimulation of moving around the world with a strong sense of love and stability inside the family.” Despite this idyllic backstory, Weaving’s parents divorced after he’d finished high school. “I’d actually left home and moved to Woolloomooloo, he recalls. “So I wasn’t damaged by it in the sense I might have been if I was 11 or 12. But it was very, very difficult for my mum and dad, and difficult for the whole family. And I was grateful that I was able, to some extent, to deal with it as a semi-adult.” Weaving was accepted directly (and unusually) into the National Institute of Dramatic Art from school. After finishing his NIDA training, he was immediately offered a two-year contract with the Sydney Theatre Company, alongside Mel Gibson and Judy Davis, Colin Friels and Ruth Cracknell. At 24, he starred in his first TV series, the 1984 smash hit Bodyline, and endeared himself to Australians everywhere by playing exactly the kind of supercilious, upper-class English villain (Test cricket captain Douglas Jardine) we most love to hate. More iconic roles followed – not overnight, but with reliable steadiness: Proof (Jocelyn Moorhouse’s 1991 low-budget gem); Priscilla in 1994; and then two Hollywood blockbuster trilogies: The Matrix from 1999; and The Lord of the Rings from 2001.



During this period, he also managed to fall in love with artist (and master Anzac biscuit maker) Greenwood and have two children, Harry (an actor, 37) and Holly (an artist, 34) Greenwood. These days, Weaving divides his time between roles in Australia and abroad (London, Ireland and New Zealand in the past couple of years), life in Sydney (he’s a passionate Sydney Swans supporter) and trips to the family property in the NSW Hunter region (where he plants gum trees and, presumably, consumes an infinite number of excellent homemade biscuits and cups of mint tea). With Cate Blanchett in Little Fish (2005). Sitting opposite him at his wide wooden table in his warm, sunlit kitchen, I’m reminded of a phrase he used years ago, in the brilliant Australian film Little Fish. Weaving plays Lionel, the father of Cate Blanchett’s Tracy, whom he calls his “shiny, shiny girl”. And at least on first impressions, this phrase seems appropriate to the scene before me now. Hugo Weaving looks like a man with a shiny, shiny life. Is it just me, or is The Airport Chaplain a terrible name for a TV show? Still, at least you know what you’re getting. Weaving plays Tobias Wallace, a kindly but enigmatic (surprise!) multi-faith-friendly fixer at Melbourne International Airport. Wallace’s average day is spent dealing with everything from dead bodies to dog poo while helping people through the most horrendously stressful drama life has to offer: attempting to board a plane. Meanwhile, of course, it’s clear he has his own horrendously stressful life drama brewing behind the scenes. Do airport chaplains actually exist? “Yes!” exclaims Weaving, leaning forward. “Do you know Jude Troy? She’s the producer. She was at Melbourne airport, and she … did she lose her passport? There was some issue like that – something quite dramatic.” In fact, Troy left her bag – with all her ID, her computer, her phone – in the back of an Uber at the airport. “Oh my god,” she says, recalling the incident. “I remember standing at the Qantas desk, totally frantic, and they introduced me to this man with ‘chaplain’ on his vest. And I was like, ‘I do not need a priest!’ ” And yet, “a few hours later I was on a flight home, bags beside me, upgraded – all thanks to this wonderful man.” No wonder she co-created and produced a TV series based on him.



Working with Weaving, Troy says, was “an honour. I know everyone says that. But he could do the role – any role, really – with his eyes closed, and yet he gave it such care and diligence. He interrogated every line, every setting, every costume – right down to how many lanyards he should wear.” “I do have this childlike interest in dress-ups,” admits Weaving: “in imaginary games, playing. But what that is, actually, is trying to put yourself in another place, transport yourself inside another human being. It’s a way of understanding the other.” This is what he’s always loved about acting. “Once I tapped into what that creative journey of acting might entail, I think I was really, really interested in it.” His preparation for roles is famously immersive. “It doesn’t always look like it’s a joy,” confessed old friend and fellow actor Richard Roxburgh recently. “I’m just aware there’s a price that he’s paying in there.” Weaving grins. “Rox is such a wonderful actor; he just wants to be in the place and play. And I do, too, but I can’t play if I don’t understand. So I will read every book, consult every source I can find.” As an actor, Weaving says, “you can’t let [your character] off the hook … but it’s not up to you to judge. It’s up to you to inhabit.” Tim Bauer This gives his characterisations real richness, say colleagues. Paula Arundell, a close friend and collaborator for more than 20 years, first saw Weaving perform in Sydney in 1995. “My first thought was ‘He’s so tall!’ ” She laughs. “And he’s so full – full and present on stage. It’s like he can gather all the little pixellations of a character and shimmeringly put them together, so you’re witnessing the full vibration of a real human being on stage in front of you – not just an outline.” “He’s always percolating,” agrees Heather Mitchell, who’s known him since they were both at NIDA in the late 1970s. “He’s never just listening and responding. He’s sharing an idea – a whole world – with you. And that makes you a better actor, because he sort of endows you with sincerity: he believes in you, he believes in the moment.”



One wonders, then, what he believes when he’s playing an objectively terrible person. In 2018, Weaving starred in Patrick Melrose, a fictionalised true story about writer Teddy St Aubyn, who was raped by his own father as a child. Weaving played this father, David Melrose. Does a role like this impinge on his own peace of mind? Weaving looks surprised. “No, not at all. It doesn’t stay with me.” He stops, thinking. “As an actor, you’re trying to embody not just the illness – this hideous, misogynist and abusive paedophile – but the human. You can’t let them off the hook, you can’t sentimentalise. But at the same time, it’s not up to you to judge. It’s up to you to inhabit. But it doesn’t mean you can’t be on set and then when it’s ‘cut’, you can’t have a laugh as Hugo. Because actually it was a very joyful set.” Weaving portraying a “hideous, misogynist and abusive paedophile” in the 2018 TV series, Patrick Melrose. Weaving loves the collegiate creativity of sets and rehearsal rooms. Back in 2012, he was – unusually for him – critical about his part in three of the four animated Transformer movies, in which he had a voice-over role as arch-villain Megatron. His ire seemed mostly self-directed: he confessed he’d never met director Michael Bay in person or read the script, and that he found his role “meaningless”. “Very rarely have I said I’d do something and I wasn’t really interested in it,” he says now. “Transformers was an example. I said no to it three times, [then] eventually I did it. But when you do make choices like that, you end up …” He pauses. “It doesn’t have the same meaning. So everything I do is something that excites me.” “He wants the work to be good. And he wants to be good,” says playwright Angus Cerini, who wrote Wonnangatta, in which Hugo starred in 2020. “He interrogates, but with real kindness.” “He has a kind of gentle command,” is how Mitchell puts it. “He thinks so deeply, not just about his role, but the whole story. He’s never forceful and never selfish, but he’s very decisive. I’ve been working with him when he’s said, ‘No, I really believe this is the way it must be. This is how I see it.’ If something’s truthful for him, he will stand by it.” Despite his success, and his dedication, you could argue acting is a strange career for Hugo Weaving. He describes himself as a “very shy, very shy little boy. Because we moved so much, I just had to experience the new place, the new school, the new house. And it was wonderful, and my eyes were continually opened. But I was also aware that I always felt like the ground underneath my feet was shifting.”

World.title: Beautiful, brilliant and forgotten: The music star who inspired Vivaldi
World.content:
The composer wrote some of his most challenging work for Anna Maria della Pieta. Violinist Augusta McKay Lodge says it’s like “a tightrope walk on strings”.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It seems only a matter of time before the story of Anna Maria della Pieta, the prodigious violinist who inspired Vivaldi, is turned into a movie. The opening scene might show a newborn being dropped off at Venice’s Ospedale della Pieta, a home for unwanted infants where the girls were trained as musicians and performed sacred music that drew audiences from across Europe. Under the cover of darkness, Anna Maria is placed in the scafetta, an opening in the ospedale’s wall. Her mother rings a bell and walks away. It’s a harsh start to life, but preferable to being drowned in a canal, the fate of many of the city’s illegitimate babies in the 18th century. Fast forward eight years and we find Anna Maria playing for the ospedale’s violin tutor Antonio Vivaldi, a red-haired Catholic priest. There are many fine musicians in Pieta’s all-female orchestra and choir – an ensemble that played, for modesty’s sake, behind metal grilles in raised galleries – but it is clear that Anna Maria is exceptional. Vivaldi procures instruments worthy of her talent and begins to write music that showcases her technical ability. An anonymous poet declares that when she played her violin “countless angels dare to hover near”. Anna Maria, opined a French scholar, was on a par with, or perhaps even better than, the masterful Italian violinist Giuseppe Tartini. Micky White, a Venice-based British researcher and the author of Antonio Vivaldi: A Life in Documents, says there is evidence to support the rave reviews. “She was an extraordinary musician who didn’t only play the violin, but other instruments such as the viola d’amore, mandolin, theorbo [a 14-string lute] and harpsichord,” she says. “These other instruments were not secondary; she was a virtuoso on all of them. She could play anything he [Vivaldi] could write for her.” Evidence of the creative relationship between the tutor and his star pupil can be found in Anna Maria’s “part book”, a red leather-bound collection of her personal repertoire now held in the library of Venice conservatory. It contains the violin parts to 26 concertos Vivaldi wrote for her; an extraordinary testament to her ability and the faith the composer of The Four Seasons placed in it. Some of that repertoire – notably the violin concerto in E major “per Anna Maria” as well as work written for her by Tartini and Pisendel – will be performed by the Australian Brandenburg Orchestra (ABO) in a recital designed to shine a spotlight on a woman who was a star in her lifetime, but relegated to a footnote by Vivaldi’s resurgence in the early part of the 20th century.



Augusta McKay Lodge, an American violinist living in Paris, will make her Australian debut as soloist and guest director and Anna Maria’s story will be narrated by NIDA graduate Lilian Alejandra Valverde from a script written by Alana Valentine. Poppy Townsend, another young NIDA graduate, has designed the lighting. Augusta McKay Lodge says the music Vivaldi wrote for Anna Maria is testament to her skill: “It’s like a tightrope walk on the strings with nothing underneath.″⁣ Lauren Desberg Related Article Sigrid Thornton Sigrid Thornton is about to play a matchmaker. This time, it’s sure to work The ABO’s co-founder and artistic director, Paul Dyer, said it was a deliberate choice to get young talent to tell Anna Maria’s story. “I sat them down and said ‘I’ve got a gift for you’,” he recalls. “It’s the story of a young woman who lived 300 years ago and has only come into the public eye in the past 15 years or so. She was abandoned, she doesn’t have a surname and she lived with all these other girls in a place where there was just one man: a red-haired priest. I said I want this story to be factual, but I want to bring it into the 21st century.” The Anna Maria revival that Dyer alludes to began, perhaps, with the rather breathlessly titled Vivaldi’s Virgins, an historical novel by Barbara Quick published in 2007. More recently, The Instrumentalist, a 2024 novel by Harriet Constable, imagines the relationship between Anna Maria and Vivaldi as a battle of wills that becomes increasingly acrimonious as the composer takes credit for his protégé’s work. Michele Riondino as Vivaldi and Tecla Insolia as Cecilia in Primavera. Meanwhile, Primavera, the debut feature of Italian director Damiano Michieletto, has Vivaldi tutoring Cecilia, a young orphan violinist who “channels” the spirit of Anna Maria. The film had its premiere at the Toronto Film Festival last year.



Anna Maria’s story lends itself to fiction because, despite her celebrity, she is something of an enigma. True, there are documents revealing details of her long life (she was 86 when she died at the Pieta on August 10, 1782), but they mostly focus on things like the purchase of her instruments or her rapid rise through the ranks (she was appointed maestra di violino and maestra di coro at the remarkably young age of 42). A 1686 engraving of the Ospedale della Pieta in Venice. De Agostini via Getty Images Sadly, there are no portraits, so we have to take the word of a poet that she was blonde, beautiful and had a “snow-white breast”. Her inner life, her thoughts about her abandonment, her relationship with Vivaldi and the reason she never left the Ospedale della Pieta despite being free to do so if she married, are unknown and open to speculation. McKay Lodge says she is reading The Instrumentalist “for fun” as she prepares for the ABO concerts. The novel “brings Anna Maria to life in a way that’s kind of hard for us to imagine just listening to the music,” she says. Related Article New music A hero to Harry Styles and Frank Ocean, the Durutti Column’s Vini Reilly is back from the brink Asked about the book’s suggestion that Vivaldi may have appropriated Anna Maria’s work, she says, “That’s only speculation. But at that time people were ‘stealing’ from each other all the time and recycling their own themes in new works. Handel is infamous for that. There was no copyright back then.” What is really unfortunate, says McKay Lodge, is the fact that none of Anna Maria’s compositions survived. “She probably was a very prolific composer and we’ll never know the extent of it.” The “extremely virtuosic” nature of Vivaldi’s compositions are a testament to Anna Maria’s ability, says McKay Lodge. Some passages include notes so high that violinists have to venture beyond the fingerboard of the instrument. “It’s like a tightrope walk on the strings with nothing underneath,” she says. Likewise, the inclusion of “big double stops”, a challenging technique where notes are played simultaneously on different strings, could also be interpreted as evidence of her technical excellence.

World.title: ‘We need to densify’: Why the 15-minute city could be the key to Melbourne’s housing crisis
World.content:
Carlos Moreno, the15-minute city pioneer, will be a keynote speaker at Melbourne Assembly, a conference The Age is hosting in October to share ideas shaping the future of our city.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne Assembly brings together the people, ideas and conversations shaping the future of our city. See all stories .

Carlos Moreno is used to defending the idea of a 15-minute city. His radical idea of bringing work, schools and essential services within a short walk of every resident has been widely adopted around the world, but it has also been weaponised by online agitators as a blueprint for government surveillance and criticised for embedding inequality. The French academic is undeterred and believes it might just be the essential, urgent prescription needed to fix Melbourne’s housing crisis. Carlos Moreno is the man behind the idea of 15-minute cities. Moreno developed the concept a decade ago as a means to a low-traffic, low-carbon future, but he says it is as relevant as ever as a way to address housing affordability and make Melbourne’s fringes more liveable. “People pushed into living far away have difficulty accessing the local services, medical services, cultural activities and educational services,” he says over a video call early in the morning from Paris, where he lives. “For this reason the 15-minute city is an amazing opportunity for transforming radically this situation.” Moreno and former New York City mayor Bill de Blasio are two of the keynote speakers at The Age’s upcoming Melbourne Assembly, which will be held in October.



Melbourne Assembly will bring together some of the world’s brightest minds across city planning, innovation, education, arts and sport to discuss ideas for Melbourne’s future. What is a 15-minute city? Moreno, who teaches at the University of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, coined the phrase “15-minute city” in 2016, and it was embraced by a group of nearly 100 mayors worldwide as a way to help recover from the COVID pandemic. A 15-minute city is a principle that everything you need should be within 15 minutes’ walk of your home – schools, shops, libraries, parks, transport, job opportunities and healthcare. The idea is that a network of 15-minute cities provides inhabitants with easy access to everything they need. If you live in a city, how long does it take you to get to a supermarket? What about a pharmacy or a school? For adherents of the 15-minute-city concept, the answer to all those questions should be “less than 15 minutes” – and it should not involve a car journey. The actual timeframe is slightly fluid: 15-minute cities are also referred to in urban planning speak as 20-minute neighbourhoods, and Copenhagen trumped everyone with a “Five Minutes to Everything” model.



The concept has provided inspiration to the City of Melbourne and the Victorian government, which implemented “20-minute neighbourhoods” in its statewide planning and development strategy Plan Victoria. “We have a global movement for implementing this idea, reducing the role of individual cars, preserving biodiversity, developing a more vibrant local economy and developing a new economical geography,” Moreno says. Related Article Note From The Editor They sought Melbourne’s Opera House and found something much better. It all started with a conversation Moreno says the lack of affordable housing near services, jobs and retail hubs makes the need to shift to 15-minute cities even more urgent. “The housing crisis is not only in the Victorian state, the question of the housing crisis is a worldwide crisis,” Moreno says. Melbourne’s urban challenge Moreno devotes a chapter of his book The 15-Minute City: A Solution To Saving Our Time And Our Planet to Melbourne, referring approvingly to it as a “pioneering” 20-minute city.



However, even Moreno concedes Melbourne’s sprawling suburbs and large “McMansions” are a barrier to creating walkable neighbourhoods. He says a mindset shift is needed to move from focusing on the importance of individual homes to prioritising sociability instead with higher-density living. He wants to see more apartments where residents spend more time out and about at libraries, local shops, cinemas and theatres instead of in cars commuting to their jobs from large homes in the outer suburbs. “We need to develop this new kind of social infrastructure for offering these new kind of services,” Moreno says. “This is today one of the rules for transforming our cities. We need to densify because the presence of the massive individual homes represent a relevant cost for us collectively.” Moreno points to the high infrastructure cost of building in greenfield outer suburbs where roads, public transport, sewerage and power all need to be installed. It’s an argument the Victorian government has deployed in designating 60 activity centres across Melbourne – including areas such as Camberwell, Brighton, Ringwood and Frankston – where it is seizing local planning controls.



Related Article Planning The inner Melbourne suburbs set for high-density housing revealed In these zones, the government controversially allows developers to bypass local councils to build high-density apartments up to 20 storeys. Moreno says he supports more development around transport links such as train stations because it helps reduce car dependency, which causes traffic jams, contributes to pollution and reduces physical activity. “We need to transform these places, we need to densify,” he says. “Low densification was the lifestyle of the 20th century, this is no longer possible in the 21st century.” Conspiracy theories and death threats Moreno’s work has attracted opposition including from what he calls “conspiracy mongers” who are concerned that 15-minute cities are really designed to restrict people’s movements so they can be better surveilled by the government. Some claim 15-minute cities represent the first step to open-air jails where residents will not be allowed to leave their prescribed area.

World.title: 49-year-old allegedly killed dog in violent attack after hitting teenage cyclists in stolen car and assaulting woman
World.content:
A man has been arrested after allegedly hitting a group of teenage cyclists in a stolen car and strangling a dog to death on a street in Auckland's Epsom.

Exact charges against the 49-year-old were still being confirmed after the series of attacks on Wednesday, police say.

Three Auckland Grammar School students were taken to hospital, one with life-threatening injuries.

Auckland City District Commander Superintendent Sunny Patel, said there was no ongoing risk to the community, but one of the teenage boys was in a critical condition in hospital and had undergone surgery.

The two other boys were in a serious and moderate condition in hospital.

The teenagers had been training as part of a cycling club, he said.

Patel said the parents of the boys had been advised and were at their sides in hospital.

What happened, according to police

Police said they were called to reports of a serious assault at the intersection of Ranfurly Road and Manukau Road about 7am.

What followed were described by Patel as six separate incidents.

Acting Detective Inspector Craig Bolton said a man without warning had assaulted a woman, causing bruising to her face, head and upper body.

"A member of the public stopped to assist the victim, before this offender has stolen the good Samaritan's vehicle," he said.

Patel confirmed the woman was jogging when she was assaulted by the man who was not wearing any pants, and three our four members of the public came to help her.

Several smashed vehicles could be seen inside the cordon RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"The offender then fled in the stolen vehicle, hitting several vehicles before striking three cyclists who were riding on Manukau Road."

After crashing the vehicle, the offender approached a woman walking her dogs.

"The offender has subjected one of the dogs to a violent assault, and sadly the dog has died at the scene," acting Detective Inspector Bolton said.

Patel said police attempted to taser the man once and then were able to taser him and pull him off the dog which had been killed.

"It is a random event that has occurred," he said.

Jessica Hopkins reports from scene of police incident in Epsom Midday Report Download MP3 2m

"This has all taken place in full view of the public going about their morning commute."

During the police standup, Patel confirmed the dog had been strangled.

Five patients were at the scene when Hato Hone St John arrived, a spokesperson confirmed.

Three cyclists were taken to hospital and two other people were treated at the scene.

The man was in police custody and Patel said charges would soon follow.

Patel said the man was known to police, but had not been on bail.

Police were assisting the dog walker, Patel said, who was "very, very upset".

Do you know more? Email iwitness@rnz.co.nz

Several smashed vehicles could be seen inside the cordon, along with a crumpled bicycle next to a red puffer jacket.

Petrol station worker Manthan Patel said he heard a "crazy" sound before he witnessed a man driving a car into another vehicle.

He said the man then got out of the car and attacked a dog.

A witness said he saw a man drive into a group of cyclists in what appeared to be a stolen car. Marika Khabazi / RNZ

A staff member at Forbes Homemade Gourmet on Ranfurly Road told RNZ she had seen the incident unfold early this morning.

"There was a guy shouting in the streets next to where I'm working.

"It seemed as though he had no pants on."

She was worried that he could come into her workplace, so decided to call the police.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Soon after, customers told cafe staff that the man had crashed a car and punched a woman, she said.

A cordon put in place around the area had caused "bumper to bumper traffic" in the area, but it was now clearing, she said.

Emergency services were called to Manukau Road around 7.05 on Wednesday morning. RNZ / Marika Khabazi
